Has your relationship with improvisation and with your own musical archive changed during those four years? A lot of water has flown since 2022. My core way of working “create a beautiful sound and try to improvise some beautiful music with it” hasn’t changed. But within that I feel like I had a lot of growth, even if that’s not something I can quantify or explain with words. I still feel the urgency to leave behind more music, both newly made and oldies. That’s the best I can offer the world, and at this point my life doesn’t have much meaning outside of that. And what made the 2016 cello improvisation “Warnings” feel particularly relevant to release in 2026, when you now hear in it “warnings from the past” about events you could not then have imagined? I’ve been making music for many years, but I only started releasing it more or less seriously in 2022. “Warnings” used to be a nameless file that surprised me every time I would dive into my older recordings and projects. It has that weird mix of urgency and mourning. It was a perfect choice to start my “Legacy Series”, because it’s a cello recording, which was the instrument that really lured me into the world of music making, and it was strong enough to stand on its own as a single. Not every release needs a story, but I find that humans seem to better connect with music that way, and I came up with a story of It being a misunderstood and ignored warning about the future invasion and darkness it brought with it. There was nothing particularly relevant to release it in 2026, other than a feeling it was time to do so, and to finally give way for other neglected music I have in store. Uncut Jams is interesting because you explicitly say you weren’t trying to demonstrate your abilities or construct a major conceptual statement—you were playing with instruments, having fun and sometimes using music as a refuge from pain. Yet you also say that removing those expectations led you towards compositional structures and sounds that you might normally have rejected as too excessive or complex. Has “not overthinking” become an increasingly important part of your practice? I don’t overthink some things and badly overthink others. For example, I like live-recorded improvisations because it condenses the aspects of composition and production into this singular realtime process, and by the end of the performance you either got it or not. It’s quite an honest way of making music. Even if I use modern technology to do that, I still have only two hands and a certain level of musical ability. At the same time, I have a relatively conceptual album project that I’ve been dragging for years, refining the concept, changing the name, adding and removing music. Just a couple of weeks ago I recorded a piece that feels like a fitting last track for it, but I’m having a hard time to apply the “no overthinking” mindset and workflow to the rest of it, as some compositions are either too complex or carry too much pain. It’s a heavy album, hopefully I have enough time to finish it. Ultimately, I treat live-recorded and produced music as two separate sonic art forms. I really love both, and I just had a new release, spiritually similar to Uncut Jams, but focused on acoustic cello improvisations. Listening back to pieces such as “Captains’ Quarters”, “Cyber Jungle”, “Daily Triumphs” and “Everything Ends Eventually”, can you hear circumstances from late 2025 entering the music despite your decision not to make the album explicitly about them? Life events and experiences inevitably inform and even bleed into my creative work, that’s a fact. With some compositions it’s quite subtle or almost non-existent, with others it gets very personal. Honestly, I wouldn’t want it any other way. In the age of so called AI and everything becoming increasingly more fake, at least I can say “Based on real events” haha) Back in 2022 you mentioned your cousin Danny as someone who had supported your music long before you were really sharing it publicly and who helped expand your musical tastes. Now that relationship has resurfaced as Thrasher Grace, but the three pieces on the album actually document an earlier period when you had limited equipment, slow computers and much less technical experience: Daniil’s voice becomes the raw material of “Mindstorm”, his eBow guitar generates “Uncertain Times”, and “Meadow” comes from an improvisation involving guitar, a smartphone used as a MIDI keyboard and a Korg controller. Why did you decide to preserve and release these recordings rather than remake them with the resources and experience you have now? “Legacy Series” is about honouring and presenting the older works as they are. I slightly remastered the audio to hopefully provide a better listening experience, but I really respect the music that I did in the past and I wouldn’t release it if that wasn’t the case. On top of that, I don’t really care about remakes. But reworking old material into something completely new is always interesting, like treating a track as a sample pack to build a new sonic narrative, which I explore sometimes. Maybe I’ll need another series of releases for that kind of thing. And does Thrasher Grace represent an archival project celebrating your shared musical past, or has rediscovering this material made you and Daniil want to create something new together? I feel I can say for both of us that properly releasing this music definitely inspired us to make something new. There’s no knowing what future Thrasher Grace might sound like, but we have plenty of instruments at our disposal, and we both have grown exponentially as musicians over the years, even if in considerably different dimensions. It’s only about us getting serious and doing the work. When we last spoke, you had only recently returned to Chernihiv after being displaced during the siege, and you described not knowing when you left in March 2022 whether you would ever see your home or family again. More than four years into the full-scale invasion, what is everyday life in Chernihiv like now, and how has your relationship with the city changed since that experience? It’s quite surreal to say this, but in retrospect that time right after the 2022 siege was quite blissful, there was a lot more hope in the air. For a few months back then life has seemed to return to a version of normal. I was also quite happy in my personal life, I was in love and probably was loved back. I’m almost nostalgic about it. Things only went downhill from there, but also a lot more nuance and depth about the war and the world has been revealed. These days the city is almost constantly in the air raid mode, and the density and success rate of the attacks seems to be increasing. It’s not a safe place to be. Upcoming winter will most likely be quite bleak, to put it mildly. But regardless if we’ll have water and heat or not, I have enough battery-powered devices to keep creating, at least for a while. In 2022 you were still able to speak about gratitude, remaining functional and building a future for yourself as an artist. Are you still able to think about the future in those terms today, and has living in Chernihiv throughout these intervening years changed what you want music — and your life as a musician — to be? It’s hard to choose an appropriate lens for this question, but maybe a few different truths can coexist. It’s not all doom and gloom, after all I was able to keep myself in one piece so far, and even in 2026 I consider myself to be blessed in many ways. But I’m 36 now, and I realise that the likelihood of me seeing 40 is quite low. I try to keep a positive outlook on life, but I live a day at the time, and any kind of future planning feels naive and futile. Considering the current trajectory of events, my best hope is making music a little while longer without any big dreams or expectations. At the same time, I appreciate my life’s story for what it is and has been so far, a really nice ride. 2026 was quite a fruitful year for me in terms of releasing music and streaming live performances, and I hope to keep and ramp up the pace going forward. Cello Drones brings you back to the instrument that, as you write, “lured” you into music more than half your life ago. The cello remains very recognisable throughout the six pieces, even as looping allows individual gestures to accumulate into drones and increasingly layered textures. What drew you back to the instrument in this particular way after years of working with synthesizers and electronics? And has your experience with electronic music changed the way you now approach the cello—particularly your sense of duration, repetition and the possibilities contained in the sustained sound of a bowed string? In a way it’s a return to the roots. My acoustic cello journey was interrupted in 2017, when I had a soundtrack project that allowed me to purchase an electric cello, which was a long dream coming true. My acoustic cello was a very cheap soviet factory made instrument, while my NS Design electric is very high-quality in terms of craftsmanship, ergonomics and playability, and overall plug-n-play experience. Shortly after this new purchase my acoustic cello fell apart (maybe out of jealousy?), the back separated from the sides and it became unplayable, and I just accepted that. For years I’ve been trying to change the sound of the electric cello into acoustic with different reverbs, impulse responses of an acoustic cello body, eq, but it was never the same. Then somewhere in summer-autumn of 2024 I decided to have my acoustic cello fixed, and everything clicked into place – both of them became two sides of the same phenomenon, similarly how electric and acoustic guitars perfectly coexist today and there’s no point in trying to convert one into another. The sounds of acoustic and electric cello actually complement each other really well. What drew me back was the sound and the physicality of the experience. I really missed the texture and variety of sonic colours and having to work it, to extract the sounds out of this mysterious wooden box with strings. I still love synths and modular and software, but you have to do a lot of work to make a really emotive synth sound, and with cello you just grab it and play away. I’m certain that years of producing electronic music serve me well now with cello. It’s quite a lo-fi sound, but despite the low quality of the instrument, my self-taught skill level and very close miking technique, I have the ability to make it somewhat pleasant, and to build sonic worlds for other people to connect with on a deeper level, even if initially I make them for myself.   SEPTMBER 10, 2026 – TALLIN Roksana Smirnova and Misha Kalinin You have been working together as a Duo for more than ten years, but you came to it from quite different musical backgrounds: Roksana through classical music and jazz, and Misha through jazz, rock, electronics and experimental music. Do you still recognise which ideas belong to one of you, or has the duo developed a language that exists somewhere between the two? Roksana: Music has been part of my life since early childhood and, in a sense, was already woven into my family. My mother and great-aunt played the piano, and my great-grandmother played the violin. I vividly remember my father calling me when I was six and asking, “Would you like to go to music school?” I immediately said yes. It was not a decision my parents made for me—it was my first independent choice connected with music. That was the beginning of my musical journey: first music school, then jazz piano at a music college in Odesa, followed by classical piano at the conservatory. Both traditions played an essential role in shaping me as a musician. In jazz, I have always been drawn to improvisation, freedom, energy, and groove; in classical music, to the richness of form, refinement, and precision. The combination of these qualities has largely shaped my own musical language. Over more than ten years, Misha and I have come a very long way creatively. We did come from different musical worlds, but we have always shared a very similar instinctive understanding of music. Of course, we each bring our own ideas, and at first we can usually recognise where a particular idea came from. But once our ideas meet, they stop existing separately and give rise to something else. I think this is how the language of our duo emerged: it draws on different styles and musical traditions, yet ultimately becomes something new that belongs to both of us. Misha: Yes, our backgrounds are different, although jazz was the common foundation for both of us in the beginning. From there, our paths developed in different directions and we each absorbed very different musical influences. In the end, that diversity has enriched our shared musical language enormously and brought many more colours into it. Over more than ten years of working together, a language of the duo has formed that now exists in its own right. It continues to transform and evolve, but it definitely has its own recognisable characteristics, colours and ways of interacting that feel specific to us. At this point, what matters most is not where an individual idea originated, but what it becomes inside that shared language. Silent Dialogues is conceived almost as a life cycle, beginning with “Inmost Dialogues” and “First Light”, passing through “Night”, “Windsong”, “Time” and “Shadows and Light”, and ending with “Memories”. At the same time, improvisation is fundamental to the way you play together. How much of that larger trajectory existed before you began recording, and how do you reconcile a clearly conceived dramatic arc with the unpredictability of improvisation? Roksana: The music for this album took its final shape during our two-month residency at the Arvo Pärt Centre in Estonia, where we had come specifically to record it. We arrived with a number of musical ideas that still needed to be developed into finished pieces, but as the process unfolded, it became clear what truly belonged on the album, what did not fit within its world, and where entirely new material needed to be created. For example, three pieces: “Time,” “When the War Is Over” and “Memories,” were written entirely during our time there. The idea of the album as a unified cycle also emerged through the process itself. We did not conceive this dramatic arc in advance—the music gradually began to find its own sequence and reveal the album’s internal logic. We do not see a carefully shaped dramatic structure and improvisation as opposites. Each composition has its own form and emotional direction, but within that framework we deliberately leave space for improvisation. It brings vitality, spontaneity, and the sense that something is being created in the here and now. In this way, the overall trajectory remains intact, while the music itself stays alive. Bringing the Laulasmaa String Quartet into the final three pieces significantly expanded the album’s sonic palette. Our musical language remained the same, but the quartet added greater depth, dimension, and new emotional colours. The strings became not simply a background or an additional layer, but another voice in the music dialogue. Misha Kalinin Misha: In earlier years, we tended to work with a larger proportion of written material and perhaps less improvisation. Over time, one of our intentions became to find the right balance between composed music and improvisation – enough structure to shape a piece, but enough openness for every performance to retain flow, freedom and the presence of the actual moment. The larger dramatic trajectory of the album gave us a frame, while improvisation allowed the music inside that frame to remain alive and unpredictable. For us, these two things are not opposites; they can strengthen each other. The Laulasmaa String Quartet enriched the sound in exactly the way we had hoped. We have always loved the colour of a string quartet and wanted to bring that dimension into the project. It also helped us expand the palette of the life cycle we were tracing throughout the album. In the final three pieces, the quartet adds another layer of depth, scale and emotional colour, and we are very happy with how naturally it became part of the duo’s sound. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Ukrainian artists have had to work in circumstances in which their nationality and the war can become almost unavoidable contexts through which their work is perceived. Do you think Ukrainian artists have any responsibility to address what is happening, or should there be complete freedom not to do so? Looking back over the past four and a half years, are there particular works of music, literature, film, visual art or theatre that you feel have captured some aspect of the experience of this war in a significant way? Roksana: From my own experience, and from what I see in the work of my Ukrainian colleagues, I do not think this is primarily a question of duty or conscious choice. I do not mean that artists have an external obligation to address the war, but rather that it becomes part of their internal creative process. A musician, artist or writer absorbs the reality around them through their own emotions and experiences, and then reflects it in their work. This is how art comes into being. It is therefore difficult to imagine a Ukrainian artist living through this reality whose work would remain completely untouched by it. At the same time, everyone expresses this experience differently. We all perceive life in our own way, so the war can appear in art in many forms – sometimes directly and explicitly, and sometimes through atmosphere, imagery or emotional tone. Over the past four and a half years, an enormous amount of music, literature, film, theatre, visual art and photography has emerged in response to the war. It is genuinely difficult for me to single out particular works, because there are so many of them and each one reflects a different aspect of this experience. Misha: The war has affected both our lives and our work very deeply. For us personally, it became a responsibility to speak about what was happening and to help bring the reality of the war to people outside Ukraine. At the same time, we were very grateful for every opportunity to represent Ukrainian culture through our duo and through our other creative projects across Europe. One important part of that work has been performing our original scores for Ukrainian silent cinema at film festivals in different countries of the European Union and in the United Kingdom. I would not single out one particular work created during the war. What has struck me more is what I have seen happening across the work of many of my colleagues. Again and again, people have gone deeper into their artistic language and revealed something new in themselves. The experience of the war has become an extremely powerful catalyst, bringing different colours, greater intensity and another level of depth into their work. In that sense, it has affected cultural figures both inside Ukraine and those now living abroad. The final section of the album contains “Peace Prelude” and “Postludia When The War Is Over”, titles that inevitably acquire particular weight coming from two Ukrainian musicians during the full-scale invasion. Could you tell us what lies behind these two compositions, and especially the decision to imagine a musical postlude to the war while the war itself is still continuing? Has the meaning of these pieces changed for you since you wrote them? Roksana Smirnova Roksana: “Peace Prelude” was inspired by the first major winter blackout in Ukraine. I remained in constant contact with my family and was deeply worried about them, because the conditions were extremely difficult. Winter days are very short, and many people were living almost entirely in darkness, without heating or even the ability to cook. What struck me most, however, was the way people responded to the situation. They did not lose heart or give up. They remained strong and continued to believe in a better future – in the light at the end of this dark tunnel. This is the hope that “Peace Prelude” expresses: hope for light in both the literal and, above all, the metaphorical sense — the belief that light will inevitably follow darkness. “Postludia When The War Is Over” grew out of an attempt to imagine what we will feel when the war finally ends. What will we feel when the explosions and gunfire fall silent, when we look at our scorched land and realise that it is truly over? Will we celebrate and dance, will we cry, will we begin to reconsider our lives — or will we experience all of these emotions at once? This postlude is therefore not simply an image of victory or a celebratory finale. It is an attempt to hear, in advance, the silence that will follow the war and to imagine the full complexity of emotions that moment will bring. Misha: Both pieces are directly connected to the war. ‘Peace Prelude’ was written by Roksana for string orchestra during a very difficult period when Ukraine was experiencing blackouts. The piece reflects a longing for peace and, at the same time, a belief that sooner or later peace will come – a peace that can bring healing, calm and restoration. “Postludia When The War Is Over” is more contemplative. It imagines the moment after the war has ended. It is almost a narrative from the perspective of an observer who is looking back at everything that has happened – the hardship, the losses, the destruction – from a point at which the war is finally over. For me, it is a kind of silent contemplation of that experience, but at its centre there is also a deep hope and belief that, with time, wounds can heal. To imagine such a postlude while the war is still continuing is, in itself, a way of looking beyond the present moment and holding on to the possibility of an ending, of peace and of healing. The titles inevitably acquire even more weight as the war continues, but the essential meaning of these pieces for me remains connected to that hope. You are both Ukrainian musicians who have spent significant periods living and working elsewhere — including Shanghai and now Berlin. After everything that has happened since 2022, what does being Ukrainian mean to each of you today? Has living outside the country altered your relationship with Ukraine, its culture and your own sense of belonging? Roksana: I think living abroad has actually made us feel our connection to Ukrainian culture more strongly, especially when we lived in Shanghai. When you live in a very different culture, you begin to feel your own roots much more clearly. A good example is “Whispers” from our first album. The piece has a very clear Ukrainian melodic character, but we did not plan this at all – it appeared naturally and spontaneously. It was interesting to see how our own culture came through in our music while we were living so far away from it. Of course, living in other countries also brings new colours and influences into our lives and our music. But our own cultural background remains the foundation. Other influences can become part of it, but the feeling of belonging to Ukrainian culture always stays with us. Misha: Since 2022, my relationship with Ukraine and its culture has become much deeper. The war became a catalyst that pushed us to go further into our own roots and to rediscover Ukrainian culture with even greater attention – its music, its cinema and its broader artistic heritage. Living outside the country has not weakened that connection. In many ways, it has made me more conscious of it. For me, being Ukrainian today means carrying a much stronger awareness of where I come from, of the culture that formed me, and of the value of those roots. The experience of these years has expanded and deepened that sense of belonging. If you were asked to assemble a small cultural portrait of Ukraine as it feels to you right now, what would each of you choose as one book, one film, one song, one album, one play, one artwork, one dish, one building, one monument and one meme? They don’t have to be canonical choices: I’m interested in what that particular combination might reveal about the Ukraine you carry with you today. Roksana: I find it difficult to think in terms of individual books, films or works of art, because any specific choice would feel too limiting. For me, Ukraine is something I experience through its nature, sounds and smells, through the way people speak, and through the taste of its wonderful fruit and vegetables. I grew up by the sea, so my image of Ukraine includes both the sound of the sea and the steppe, as well as the smell of dry grass and sun-warmed earth in summer. I do not think any single work of art could fully capture this image. So if I were to create a cultural portrait of Ukraine, it would not be a list of ten specific things, but rather a mosaic of sounds, scents, flavours, landscapes and memories. Misha: It is genuinely difficult for me to reduce Ukraine to one choice in every category. Because we are from Odesa, so many of my strongest associations are naturally connected with the city. Rather than force a list of ten cultural references, I would choose two things that feel immediate and essential to me right now. The dish would be Ukrainian borshch. The building would be the Odesa Opera House. They are very different symbols, but together they connect something deeply everyday and familiar with the cultural memory and beauty of the city I come from.   SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 – KYIV photo by Anna Reznik Forma Formanta Could you begin by telling us about your musical background and how Forma Formanta came into being? When I was around 17, I formed a band where we played something somewhere between psychedelic rock, shoegaze, and post-punk. After the band broke up, I started trying to write music on my own, around seven years ago. My introduction to experimental music began, as it often does at a young age, with an interest in the London esoteric underground. After that I just kept digging and listening to a lot of different things, but probably mostly ambient and dark ambient, drone noise, and dark folk. I’d loved things like darkwave, coldwave, post-punk, and synthwave since I was a kid — that kind of music had always been with me. But up to a certain point, I really disliked dealing with rhythmic parts. I preferred working with samples I recorded myself and with synthesizers, without being tied to a linear rhythm. I still have much more material like that, and I associate it with my om nyolc project, which doesn’t have any fixed genre direction, sound, or particular vector. If we’re talking about projects that influenced the sound which later separated into Forma Formanta, then it was discovering Hype Williams, some projects released on Northern Electronics and Posh Isolation, as well as hypnagogic pop / darkwave projects like Plecid and Tollund Men. Eventually I came to realise that what I love most is music that is extremely simple in terms of form and harmony, often with intentionally shitty recording quality. That kind of sound creates a feeling of carelessness, vagueness, and the lightness of dreams, and because the form itself is so simple, it becomes easier to work with different kinds of content within it. Zahid was recorded between Vienna and Kyiv from 2021 to 2025, spanning the period immediately before and after Russia’s full-scale invasion. You describe it as reflecting the loss of a foundation or axis — something that might be called “home” — while also connecting that feeling to a wider state of turbulence and increasing entropy. How did the album and your understanding of “home” change during those four years? Did material begun before February 2022 acquire meanings afterwards that you could never have anticipated? For a year before the war began, I lived in Vienna, where some of the first material that ended up on the album was written. It was an interesting experience, but not the most pleasant one — like almost any experience of emigration, I think. It’s natural to want to return to a sense of familiarity and stability, and generally to somewhere that feels like “your place.” With those expectations, I came back to Kyiv a couple of weeks before the full-scale invasion began. My understanding of “home” hasn’t really changed over that time. What changed is that I stopped trying to recreate it, find it, or get it back, even as a kind of fantasy. Maybe at the beginning some people still thought that things could somehow go back to the way they were, but I think by now everyone understands that there is no “before” to return to. It’s not exactly a new thought. The material written during those years started to contain more motifs of endings, finality, and completion. Not in a pessimistic sense, like everything is over and nothing good will happen anymore, but almost the opposite — as a way of living through it, making space to move further, accepting whatever happens, “learning how to swim.” Of course, this idea of “losing the ground beneath your feet,” both literally and figuratively, has accumulated more and more meaning and intensity over time. But I don’t even want to try to extrapolate what this musical material means to me personally onto the events of the past few years. Those events are too vast and too heavy, and I’m definitely not in a position to comprehend them to any meaningful extent. The liner notes compare remembering home to trying to recall a dream after waking, where details gradually disappear and imagination fills the blank spaces. That process seems embedded in the music itself: raw, muted textures in which simple elegiac melodies emerge briefly and then recede. How did you translate this movement between memory, forgetting and imagination into sound? And how do the album’s titles — from “apparition” and “death will disappear” to “sleep with armors of defeated knights” and “elegy” — fit into that world? If we’re talking about the more technical ways of moving from dream or imagination into a sonic modality, then things like distorting the original signal, using raw drone textures, or burying the vocals in noise until very little is intelligible are all fairly standard tools that have been used by many artists. Maybe the only difference is that I tried to push them into something even rawer, noisier, and more careless than is usually considered acceptable. Apart from that, I used the Soviet TOM 1501 synthesizer on almost every track. It has this very broad and deep string sound which, for me personally, is already associated with something pleasant and forgotten (and no, I don’t mean the usual nostalgia about ice cream costing five kopeeks or anything like that). As for the titles, some of them refer to words or phrases that actually appear in the tracks. They’re not really intelligible to the listener, but it matters to me what is there. The rest can come from images taken directly from dreams, or from invented, absurd combinations of words that are still meant to convey a certain image. For example, one of the tracks that carries many of these motifs of endings and completion, “moon cycle flavor mix,” got its title because I was amused by the World Ice Theory of the Austrian pseudo-scientist Hanns Hörbiger. He had this hypothesis that there had previously been four moons, three of which eventually fell to Earth, each time bringing an era to an end, destroying most living things, and beginning a new age. To this idea of global cycles, endings, and renewals, I added the name of a cigarette I used to really like and with which I have some associations, but which disappeared from sale around eight years ago: Marlboro Flavor Mix. You live in Kyiv. What is everyday life in the city like for you now, after more than four years of full-scale war? How have attacks, air-raid alerts, power disruptions and the cumulative exhaustion of the war affected your daily routines and your ability or desire to make music? At the same time, what continues to make Kyiv a place you want to live in and call home? I don’t think it would be appropriate to talk about my own exhaustion in particular. My daily routine has also remained more or less the same throughout these years. The main difference is probably that I go to concerts and other events much less often now. As for music and creativity, yes, the last two or three years have been more difficult. There’s less desire, and less enjoyment even in simply listening to the things that used to inspire me or in looking for new music. In 2022–23 I still had occasional bursts of energy — new ideas would appear, I started new musical projects together with friends, we even played some kind of post-hardcore for a while. Then, for a number of reasons, all of that gradually faded. Even though I used to love Kyiv incredibly much, it has increasingly become a place where I don’t really want to live anymore. At the moment, I simply don’t have the possibility to move elsewhere. And it’s not even mainly because of the attacks. It has more to do with the terrible transport infrastructure, roadworks that can last for years on a single stretch, ugly development (often illegal) and the destruction of green areas, parks, small public gardens, and historic architecture. The list could go on. Ideally, I think I’d probably prefer to live somewhere more rural not far from Kyiv, or in a city two or three times smaller. At the same time, I still of course consider Kyiv my home, and I hope that at some point the situation will change for the better and it will become a comfortable place to live in again. Has the experience of the past four years changed what being Ukrainian means to you personally? In terms of country, identity, and so on, almost nothing has changed for me over the past four years. I think most of my answers to those questions had already formed during the period when I lived outside Ukraine. I can’t really call myself a patriot. What I understood is simply that this is my place, and I want it to continue existing — with these people and on this territory. The main thing that exists here, and that seems to be gradually disappearing elsewhere, is freedom. Very little is regulated here to any serious extent. You can be who you want to be and do what you want to do. Of course, wartime introduces certain corrections to that, but I don’t think they are fundamental or permanent changes. I think this place quite rightfully fits the word “volnytsia” — and I’m not sure there is really an adequate English equivalent for it. It implies a kind of unruly freedom, a space where people are difficult to govern or contain. I like the fact that it is hard to call us barbarians, but we are definitely not modern Western civilization either. It is a frontier, and on many levels, not only socially or politically. There are certainly things here that are completely surreal and absurd, but at the same time it feels like one of the few places where you can still encounter something genuinely alive and real. Looking at Ukrainian music specifically, are there any albums released since 2022 that have captured the experience of the country particularly meaningfully for you — perhaps expressing something about the war or contemporary Ukrainian life that news reports and political language cannot? To be honest, I can’t point to anything specific — some complete artistic statement that really affected me in that way. Maybe this is partly because, as I mentioned earlier, I generally listen to less new music now, and things don’t affect me as strongly as they used to. In my modest opinion, there were more powerful releases and projects in the period between 2014 and 2021, also against the background of a strengthening Ukrainian identity and the political events surrounding it. Or maybe now there is simply so much happening that I can’t single things out from the general flow anymore. I’m not sure. But I’m very impressed by the overall sense of collective momentum — by the fact that under these conditions people continue doing an enormous amount of work. Experimental music in particular has developed very noticeably; before, it existed much more on the margins compared to more conventional electronic music. I like what Kyivpastrans Records and Erythroleukoplakia are doing, projects like Radio Rukh, 20ft, the regular organisation of experimental events, and the fact that there are teams bringing interesting international artists to Ukraine and organising concerts across the country, such as Obscure Bookings. I also really like the amount of attention being given to rediscovering, archiving, and popularising different kinds of Ukrainian music. Maybe this particular growth of experimental genres and events is itself an attempt to express the chaos people are living through. This is symmetrical to the way in which music, in turn, connects to the listener. Today, it is difficult even to perceive the difference between these two connections, but once there was an enormous distance between them. A singer taking part in the performance of a Josquin Mass presupposed a trajectory of sound that did not lead to the listener, because the figure of the listener did not exist in the church in the first place. Even when members of the congregation were present at the service, the singers were either isolated from them or turned away from them; combined with the church’s powerful reverberant acoustics, this effectively deprived the congregation of the possibility of perceiving the music. If we set aside the liturgical function and the metaphysical dimension of the process, and consider instead the physical and physiological dimension of musical practice, music here returned to itself, existing in a reflexive loop. The sound produced by the singer returned to the singer and shaped a state in which he could produce sound that was even more effective at producing the state in which effective sound could be produced. The circular trajectory of the music enclosed and isolated the musical material. When we encounter Josquin’s music, we immediately register the autonomy and coherence of its sonic construction. In terms of expression, it is alien to the kind of expressivity we habitually describe as a reliance on an outward effect. When we listen to Josquin’s music today, we connect to it asymmetrically. The singers’ voices always seem to come, so to speak, from afar; they do not address us directly. We always listen from the side, in a sense eavesdropping, witnessing the circular trajectory of the music and the effect that sound, through the singer’s body, has upon itself. In working on this piece, I sought to reproduce this ancient circular trajectory of sound. This also determined the insufficiency, and ultimately the inadequacy, of a linear algorithm in which the score is realized in a single act: a direct performance, fixed in a recording and aimed at the listener. I needed to submit to the effect of the sound and, in turn, affect it under the influence of that effect. Having accepted these rules, in the course of realizing the piece in sound I substantially altered and supplemented the performance of the original score with sounds of different origins. In other words, I intervened in its realization by virtually every means through which a composer can directly influence the sonic result—from field recordings to sound samples, to the creation of autonomous musical structures and events within this new sonic environment. These almost always conceal the initial material, making it nearly indistinguishable within the texture of the final sound. Nevertheless, it was precisely this initial impulse, at the origin of the circular trajectory, that determined the character and rhythm in which the spiral of this music unfolds. I am sincerely grateful to all the musicians through whom Fernstimmen—“distant voices”—have come closer.   DJ POPS ~ между частотами The label ERYTHROLEUKOPLAKIA out of Kyiv presents itself in a raw, punky style, but this second album from associate DJ Pops is altogether more considered and delicate than you might be expecting. It’s another one with IDM/braindance irregularity at its core, but it’s definitely got more emphasis on the “dance” side of the equation; so no matter how lopsided the grooves might get, they nonetheless are grooves, and hold the attention and the body locked in. It also, however abstract it gets, feels weirdly un-digital—like constructions of wood, string, rusty metal, tape, and glue, sometimes with little creatures running around inside them. [Bandcamp Daily]   MIXES   VIEWING ROOM (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Alxrm — The beginning of the real Rush - no offense to John Rutsey and the debut album which I really like- but Geddy and Alex ever since were aspiring for a deeper sound and a more progressive direction which didn't appeal to John. This is made plain even from the intro of the opener of the album which actually was the jamming they did together when Neil was auditioning for the band. Even though the music remains essentially rock and most song durations are around the three-minute mark, the first twists and turns make the presence felt. More than that, acoustic (Fly by Night, In the End) and classical (Rivendell) guitars are tastefully used to widen their palette of sound. However, the key-track on the album is the suite By-Tor & The Snow Dog because its complex structure would become their compass for the future where they would go off their pure rock roots entirely.Compared to the debut, the listener can easily perceive the growth the band underwent within such a short amount of time. The unstrained enthousiasm is replaced by deeper and at times more complex compositions showing clearly that the boys would not content themselves by repetition. Moreover, the new guy would become their standard lyricist and would go down in history as one of the best of all time. We should thank our luck that their paths were crossed.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — If you have followed my reviews spanning the prog folk diaspora, you'll know there is nothing I welcome less than another version of "Scarborough Fair", with which particularly Nordic groups seem disproportionately enamored. It therefore follows that I cannot recommend an album in which arguably the best track is in this single-song sub genre. Sadly this is the case for the extinct-on-arrival dinosaur known now as the "Kaarmesormus". It might garner 3 stars from a new group just based on the continued mellotron blasts but not from esteemed veterans like KOSMOS, and, while each number could be a supporting cast on a better album, this isn't that. From the soporific first half to the plodding and equally exhausted faux metal second half with its SSRI-free spoken interludes, this is all a big downer, and I do normally appreciate the authentically morose. If I had to pick a couple they would be the opener and "Kielletyn hedelm�n tarha", but both are essentially submerged in their surroundings. Like a therapist once said to a friend who cried incessantly through the first few sessions, "you need a good drug". Start anywhere else and let this one slither off to the side until you are emotionally ready. 2.5 stars rounded down.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Undoubtedly one of the great surprises of this year is the release of King Gizzard's full-blown EDModyssey 'Alien Metal', which is their twenty-eight studio album to date. The follow-up to 2025's'Phantom Island' sees the Australian band abandoning all rock instrumentation for a futuristic beat-driven, techno-inspired rave sound, utilizing a modular synth system that allows them to explore avast range of sequenced rhythms, electronic textures, and an overall synthetic, club-orientedproduction style. Contemporary bands rarely do such dramatic stylistic shifts, but this acid-ladencreation from the kings of psychedelic blues turns out to be a fun and engaging listen (that willnevertheless shock many dedicated fans), that is above all else, a finely constructed electronicwork, wherein each tracks flows into the next one, giving the impression of a massive piece ofprogressive house. Within this mixture of quirky techno beats, bassy breakbeats, and ambientinterludes, the ominous alien-like robotic vocals that wiggle their way through, give 'Alien Metal'somewhat of a sci-fi edge. However, despite all of the pristine synth sequences and polished studiosound, the occasional repetitiveness of this album can potentially lead to listener fatigue.Moreover, the synthetic club feel provides for a great background listen, but is there really thatmuch substance to dig into upon repeated listens? The tracks that I enjoy the most on 'Alien Metal'are the punchy opener 'Sapience', which beautifully transitions into the excellent title track,followed by the powerful and mesmerizing 'Level 5', and the trippy 'Uqt', which appears towards theend. The album finale is strong, too, while the entire work feels intentionally futuristic andvibrant, which is perhaps what most listeners would cling to.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — This might be the first time I have not been taken aback by a new Mastodon album, simply because theexpectations have been exceedingly high this time around. A reflection upon the dramatic passing offounding member Brent Hinds, following his departure from the band earlier, 'Marrow Deep' is arecord exploring grief through a variety of dense and ominous sounds. This is not necessarily areturn to the extreme and primal energy that had shaped the Atlanta-based band's early records, butit comes close to being their most straightforward metal album in years. Having added touringguitarist Nick Johnston and keyboardist Jo�o Nogueira to the lineup, this five-piece version ofMastodon is intriguing, but it lacks the untamed songwriting of Brent Hinds and his overtlypsychedelic undercurrents. For this reason, 'Marrow Deep' is somewhat less adventurous thanpreceding releases from the band, even if it preserves the sludge-informed prog metal framework thatlisteners have become accustomed to. It just feels solid all throughout but without significantpeaks.Production-wise, this album is strong but not groundbreaking, with the heavy guitars occupying mostof the mix. I do, however, vastly enjoy the prominent contributions of the band's full-time keyboardplayer, whose playing provides a beautiful atmospheric backdrop to the otherwise ravaging guitars ofBill Kelliher and Nick Johnston. Interestingly enough, there is a greater highlight on melodictextures and sombre passages on 'Marrow Deep', that had only been superficially explored on 'Hushedand Grim'. Nevertheless, this new Mastodon record feels meandering without really having any weakmoments. Highlight tracks like the fast-paced 'Snakes for Dinner', the ritualistic sludgy number'They're Coming for You', and the tasteful but melancholic song 'The Vanishing', featuring GeezerButler and reminiscent of the great 'Planet Caravan', are perhaps the only moments worth lookingforward to upon repeated listens, while monotonous heavy numbers like 'Poisonous Weapons' and 'Inthe Ruins' lack the novel and mind-bending edge that used to make each new Mastodon something toanticipate.Longtime fans of the band will discover heaps of excellent, wild and turbulent riffs here, while theenjoyers of the band's progressive leanings shall be pleased with the haunting keyboards appearingon 'Marrow Deep'. Consistent and straightforward, this record hardly reinvents the Mastodon sound,which is very likely why it doesn't fully click with me.

items.body: “Tadzungaira” is one of the old Shona mbira pieces, played at ceremonies when a family calls on its ancestors to end a run of hardship: a drought, a stretch of poverty, a season where nothing comes right. The word means we are lost, and some traditional players refer to the piece as “Todzungaira”, others as “Muroro” or “Nehondo”. The Mbira Renaissance Band played it at Paper Birch Books in Edmonton on 21 February. They have reached for the word before: “Daira”, from their 2018 album Famba, has the line “Tadzungaira, tadzungaira musango”, we are tired, we have been wandering in the forest a long time. The song opened their session for the Pocket-Sized Series, a monthly recording run by the band’s drummer, Tony Flanagan, made among the shelves of the bookshop and released as video, modelled on Tiny Desk and funded by the Edmonton Arts Council. The Mbira Renaissance Band came out of the Canadian city’s music scene in 2013, started by mbira player Chaka Zinyemba with bassist James Stuart. Chaka and lead singer Chiedza Zinyemba are from Zimbabwe and sing in Shona, with Chiedza also on hosho and congas. George Koufogiannakis plays guitar and brings thirty years of jazz behind it, Flanagan drums, and Munya Viyali is on keys. Their repertoire sets the mbira alongside jazz, reggae and afro-pop, and the songs are usually about family and coming together. They toured Zimbabwe for the first time in July 2025 and released the album Roto the following January: half of its eight tracks carry a horn section with parts written by Koufogiannakis, “Zunza” brings in West African djembe from Reckie Lloyd and closes on mbira, and “Mufaro” features the Afro-Cuban duo OKAN with pianist Jeremy Ledbetter. Stream, listen to and get your copy of Roto HERE The post Daily Discovery: The Mbira Renaissance Band – Tadzungaira appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: French post-industrial project Dernière Volonté releases its new album, “Cendre”, on 25 September 2026, in digipak CD, black vinyl and a limited edition of 250 copies on translucent crystal-blue vinyl. “Cendre” returns to the dense, nocturnal and melancholic atmosphere of Dernière Volonté’s earliest work, revisiting the industrial and dark ambient tone the project carried before its shift toward song-based writing on “Les Blessures de l’Ombre” in 2003 and “Devant le Miroir” in 2006. The twelve tracks are “Harmonies”, “Vanités”, “Maudits”, “Mandoline”, “L’Âne et le Roi”, “Ombres”, “Des Questions”, “Contre Jour”, “Les Jets de Pierres”, “Plus j’y pense”, “Les Jardins de Tannhäuser” and “Célébration (bien à toi)”. The crystal-blue vinyl edition comes with a printed innersleeve and a download code, while the CD edition ships in a 16-page booklet. “L’Âne et le Roi” is the second track shared ahead of the album, following “Célébration (à toi…)”. Both tracks carry forward the martial rhythms, electronics and voice that have defined the project’s sound since the 1990s, applied here to the darker, sparer arrangements of Dernière Volonté’s formative albums. Dernière Volonté’s extended back catalogue remains available alongside the new album, including “Cristal”, “Commémoration”, “Devant le Miroir”, “Frontière”, “Immortel”, “Le Feu Sacré”, “Mon Meilleur Ennemi”, “Ne Te Retourne Pas” and “Prie pour Moi”. About Dernière Volonté Dernière Volonté is the project of French musician Geoffroy Delacroix, known publicly as Geoffroy D., formed in the mid-1990s. The project’s debut release, “Obéir et Mourir”, arrived in 1998 as a limited cassette rooted in martial industrial and dark ambient, built on militaristic rhythms, historical samples and sparse vocals. “Le Feu Sacré” followed in 2001, still within that early industrial and dark ambient mode. Dernière Volonté’s sound changed direction with “Les Blessures de l’Ombre” in 2003, which applied the project’s martial rhythms to verse-chorus song structures and pop melodies for the first time. “Devant le Miroir” continued that shift in 2006, combining drums, synthesizers and dark textures with more intimate melodies. Geoffroy Delacroix expanded his output in 2008 with Position Parallèle, an electronic side project with Pierre Pi mixing EBM and minimal wave, which has released five studio albums to date including “Néons Blancs” (2013), “En Garde à Vue” (2017) and “Aiguille à Découdre” (2024). Dernière Volonté’s own discography continued with “Immortel” (2010), “Mon Meilleur Ennemi” (2012), “Prie pour Moi” (2016), “Frontière” (2019) and “Cristal” (2022). With “Cendre”, the project returns to the darker, more atmospheric register of its first records while keeping the melodic voice it built up over three decades.

items.body: Swiss electronic musician Carlos Perón and German industrial project Melting Rust Opera released their debut full-length collaboration, “Ultra Haunted Overdrive”, on 7 August 2026 through Dark Daze Music. The ten-track album follows two prior joint singles, “Start Again” and “I’m a Ghost”, and gathers a further eight tracks the pair produced over roughly a year of work. Perón produced the album’s tracks, while Melting Rust Opera’s Stefan Bahners handles vocals and lyrics throughout. “Ultra Haunted Overdrive” runs just under 43 minutes and opens with “Quick and Dirty”, followed by “I’m a Ghost”, “An Other Crime”, “Get the Night Out of Your Head”, “Clean Up”, “It’s Not OK”, “The Disasters We Face”, “I Will Adore You”, “Start Again” and the closing “One Star”. The record brings an industrial rock sound that mixes aggressive guitar structures with electronic production and noise elements, moving between brutal and melancholic registers across its ten tracks. The two singles carried over from earlier releases were both already covered on Side-Line: “I’m a Ghost” appeared as a standalone single on 10 December 2025, and “Start Again”, produced by Perón with vocals and lyrics from Bahners, opened the collaboration on 2 May 2025. A third advance track, “An Other Crime”, followed as a single on 13 March 2026 before landing on the album. Carlos Perón and Melting Rust Opera’s collaboration history Perón and Melting Rust Opera had already worked together before their first joint single. Perón contributed to “Manipuliert – Carlos Peròn Trümmer Mischung” on Melting Rust Opera’s 2023 EP “Neue Trümmer”, and mastered the band’s 2024 album “The Power Of I Don’t Care”, also released on Dark Daze Music. “Ultra Haunted Overdrive” is the first release credited jointly to both acts as a full-length collaboration. About Carlos Perón Carlos Perón is a Swiss electronic musician from Zurich, one of the three founding members of the legendary Swiss synth-pop trio Yello, formed with Boris Blank and Dieter Meier in 1979. He left the group in 1983 to pursue a solo career spanning electronic experiments, film soundtracks and conceptual releases on labels including Ralph Records, Dark Daze Music and SPV. Early solo works include “Impersonator” (1981) and the soundtrack “Die Schwarze Spinne” (1983), followed by a series of conceptual releases through the 1990s and 2000s. Perón founded the Eisenberg label in the late 1980s and launched the “Der Eisenberg Sampler” compilation series, later revived with Norwegian label Sub Culture Records. He also works as a producer and mastering engineer, having worked with acts including Punch ‘n’ Judy and Piston Damp, and with Beborn Beton in Switzerland and Cologne. Through 2025 and into 2026, Perón has released a run of metal-leaning singles under his Dark Daze Music imprint, alongside his ongoing work with Melting Rust Opera. About Melting Rust Opera Melting Rust Opera is an experimental industrial and metal project based in Rheinbach, Germany, centered on musician and producer Stefan Bahners, with Wilson May contributing live percussion. The project emerged in late 2016 or early 2017 after Bahners’ earlier project, Die Rostigen Löffel, went on hiatus, and combines industrial, avant-garde and noise elements with rock and metal structures. Melting Rust Opera’s discography includes the full-lengths “The Rise and Fall of Flesh Wire” (2021) and “different places” (2022), the EP “Neue Trümmer” and the release “Broken Zukunft” in 2023, and “The Power Of I Don’t Care” (2024). The project has also released remix work, including a version of Laibach’s “Bossanova” (2017), two remixes for Dagobert’s single “Das Mädchen aus der schönen Welt”, a remix of Anne Clark’s “Orange Suns” for “Synaesthesia – Classics Reworked”, and a remix of A Place To Bury Strangers’ “I’m Hurt” for “See Through You: Rerealized”. “Ultra Haunted Overdrive” extends the project’s ongoing work with Perón into its first joint album.

items.body: The March Violets reissue “Turn to the Sky” b/w “Miss Amanda Jones” on digital services on September 18, 2026, and have added a second run of tour dates across the UK, continental Europe and Brazil. The English post-punk and gothic rock band released “Turn to the Sky” as a single in February 1986 on London Records, and the version now being reissued is the re-recording made the following year for the John Hughes film “Some Kind of Wonderful.” The reissue pairs that 1987 film version of “Turn to the Sky” with “Miss Amanda Jones,” a cover of the Rolling Stones song that the band recorded for the same soundtrack. Both tracks had previously been available only on the film’s soundtrack album. Producer Stephen Hague, working from the band’s 1986 original, re-recorded “Turn to the Sky” for the film, and the band performed the song on screen, spending two weeks on the production’s Hollywood set. “Some Kind of Wonderful,” directed by Howard Deutch and written and produced by John Hughes as a follow-up to his 1986 hit “Pretty in Pink,” stars Lea Thompson as Amanda Jones, the character the film’s title track and the Rolling Stones cover both reference. The tour, billed as the second leg of the “Unnatural History” run, follows 14 UK dates the band played in June and July 2026 in support of their “Natural History” album reissue. Alongside that 1980s catalogue, the band also performs songs from Crocodile Promises, their 2024 album, and have said a further album is half-finished. Tour dates for The March Violets October 27, 2026 – Prague, Czechia – Lucerna Music Bar October 31, 2026 – Whitby, UK – Tomorrow’s Ghosts Festival, Pavilion Theatre November 1, 2026 – Newcastle-upon-Tyne, UK – The Cluny November 3, 2026 – Edinburgh, UK – Speakeasy November 5, 2026 – Derby, UK – The Hairy Dog November 6, 2026 – Huddersfield, UK – Amped November 8, 2026 – Bedford, UK – Esquires November 10, 2026 – London, UK – New Cross Inn November 11, 2026 – Brighton, UK – Komedia February 6, 2027 – Sao Paulo, Brazil – Wave Festival Ticket and merchandise links for the dates are listed on the band’s official site. About The March Violets The March Violets formed in Leeds in December 1981, when guitarist Tom Ashton, bassist Laurence “Loz” Elliott, and singers Simon “Detroit” Denbigh and Rosie Garland met at Leeds University. Sisters of Mercy singer Andrew Eldritch released the band’s debut EP, “Religious as Hell,” on his Merciful Release label on August 28, 1982. Seven March Violets singles reached the UK Indie Chart, and the 1984 compilation “Natural History” reached number three on that chart. Cleo Murray replaced Garland as the band’s main vocalist from the 1983 single “Snakedance” onward. In 1986 the band signed to the major label London Records and released “Turn to the Sky,” written by Murray, Elliott and Ashton, as its final single before splitting. The band, by then made up of Ashton, Elliott, drummer Andy Tolson and Murray, went on to record and perform “Turn to the Sky” and “Miss Amanda Jones” for the 1987 film “Some Kind of Wonderful.” The band reunited in 2007 for a one-off Leeds show with Denbigh, Garland and Ashton, joined by Matt Thorpe (of Isolation Division) on bass, and reformed again in 2010. That lineup of Garland, Ashton and Thorpe released a five-CD boxset in 2022 and the album Crocodile Promises on Metropolis Records on July 19, 2024. The reissue of “Turn to the Sky” and “Miss Amanda Jones,” and the new tour dates announced alongside it, follow that album and this year’s “Natural History” reissue and its accompanying UK tour.

items.body: New Zealand electronic rock band Robots In Love will release “Cease and Desist” on September 25, the second single from their upcoming album OVERRIDE. The Dunedin-based act is the creative partnership of vocalist and producer Elenor Rayner and drummer and producer Alex Burchell, joined again by guitarist Henry Flynn Wall of Rebirth To Ruin, who also featured on their previous single, “Convergence”. “Cease and Desist” is a melodic industrial track about extreme obsession. Rayner said she recently discovered the word “limerence” and began thinking about the inability to control obsession, which led to the line “limerence closes every door“, describing a state where no amount of reasoning can get through. Musically, the track scales back its verses before building into a chorus built on heavier riffs. The single also carries two remixes. Melbourne cyberpunk act Sirus contributes a version that moves through decades of electronic music, opening with an ’80s-style sound, passing through a ’90s R&B-inspired interlude and closing on darker, more futuristic production. Burchell also remixes the track under his own alias, Magnetique, in a more subversive take. “Cease and Desist” follows “Convergence”, released on June 8, 2026 as the lead single from OVERRIDE. “Convergence” has drawn over 41,000 YouTube views and 14,000 Spotify streams, and Robots In Love have paired “Cease and Desist” with an official video as well. About Robots In Love Robots In Love is the New Zealand electronic rock project of vocalist and producer Elenor Rayner and drummer and producer Alex Burchell, based in Dunedin (Ōtepoti). The current lineup came together in 2023, with Rayner and Burchell also working separately on other projects: Rayner has released material as Sobriquet and The Crystalline Effect, while Burchell drums with Angels Unchained and the Dunedin Symphony Orchestra and produces under the name Magnetique. The band mixes industrial rock, dark electro, drum and bass, trip hop, goth, metal and cyberpunk influences into a sound built on layered vocals, heavy guitars and electronic production. Side-Line has followed the band’s release history since 2022, when Robots In Love, then working as a New Zealand-based dark electro act, teamed up with Swedish producer JA/VI. They premiered the “Gossip In Your Head” video in September 2023, followed by an EP and remix video that November. In April 2024, the band premiered the “Unbreakable” video, and in January 2025 followed with the “Crush” video. Robots In Love released their debut album, “Activate!”, on May 23, 2025, reaching number 17 on the Aotearoa chart. “Convergence” arrived in June 2026 as the first single from OVERRIDE, with “Cease and Desist” now set to follow it on September 25.

items.body: Dead Can Dance, the British-Australian neoclassical darkwave duo formed in Melbourne, released “Into the Labyrinth” on 13 September 1993 through 4AD. The album turns 33 this year. It was their sixth studio album, the first they recorded without any guest musicians, and the first to get a major-label release in the United States, through 4AD’s distribution deal with Warner Bros. Records. It went on to sell more than 500,000 copies worldwide and made the duo 4AD’s highest-selling act. Recording ‘Into the Labyrinth’ at Quivvy Church Lisa Gerrard and Brendan Perry had separated domestically in 1989. Perry was living in County Cavan, Ireland, Gerrard in Australia, and the two wrote their material apart. Gerrard then travelled to Perry’s studio, a converted church at Quivvy, where they merged the songs and recorded the album across three months. Perry engineered and produced it there. Every instrument on the record is played by the two of them, including bongos, sitar and tabla. Gerrard sings in English on tracks 2 to 4, 8 and 11, and uses her wordless vocal technique on tracks 1, 5 to 7, 9 and 10. Tracks 3 and 10 were performed a cappella. Two of the eleven tracks are not the duo’s own writing. “The Wind That Shakes the Barley” is a late 18th-century Irish ballad with words and music by Robert Dwyer Joyce, arranged by the band. Gerrard explained in the album’s press kit why she wanted to record it: “it was meant to be a rallying song, but it has such an intense sadness that it becomes an anti-war song”. The closing “How Fortunate the Man With None” sets four stanzas of Bertolt Brecht’s 1928 poem “Die Ballade von den Prominenten”, in John Willett’s English translation, to music Perry wrote for a Temenos Academy production of the play. It was only the second time the Brecht estate had granted such permission, the first being in 1963. Perry described “The Ubiquitous Mr Lovegrove”, the album’s single, as his alter ego, “the abstract relationship of myself and woman”. The title comes from a 1965 episode of the TV series “Danger Man”. 4AD assembled a video for “Yulunga (Spirit Dance)” using footage from the film “Baraka”. The eleven tracks run “Yulunga (Spirit Dance)”, “The Ubiquitous Mr Lovegrove”, “The Wind That Shakes the Barley”, “The Carnival Is Over”, “Ariadne”, “Saldek”, “Towards the Within”, “Tell Me About the Forest (You Once Called Home)”, “The Spider’s Stratagem”, “Emmeleia” and “How Fortunate the Man With None”. In the UK the CD arrived alongside a limited double vinyl LP that added “Bird” and “Spirit”, the two bonus tracks from the 1991 compilation “A Passage in Time”. Touhami Ennadre supplied the cover photograph, “Hands of the World”; Chris Bigg designed the sleeve with Perry, and Ken Kavanagh shot the booklet images. The US release followed on 14 September 1993. About Dead Can Dance Dead Can Dance formed in Melbourne in August 1981 as a trio, with Brendan Perry on vocals and guitar, Paul Erikson on bass and Simon Monroe on drums. Lisa Gerrard, previously of Microfilm, joined on vocals and percussion. Perry and Gerrard had met through Melbourne’s Little Band scene. Their first official recording, a home version of “Fatal Impact”, appeared on the December 1981 issue of the cassette magazine Fast Forward. After a farewell show at St Kilda’s Crystal Ballroom in May 1982 the pair moved to London and signed to 4AD, with Erikson and Peter Ulrich completing the first UK line-up. The self-titled debut arrived in February 1984, its sleeve built around a New Guinea ritual mask, and sat close to the ethereal wave of labelmates Cocteau Twins. The EP “Garden of the Arcane Delights” followed in August. From “Spleen and Ideal” (November 1985), co-produced with John A. Rivers and scored for cello, trombone and timpani, the duo turned towards the medieval and Renaissance material that became their signature; the album reached number 2 on the UK indie chart. Dead Can Dance’s ‘Within the Realm of a Dying Sun’ came in 1987, “The Serpent’s Egg” in 1988 and “Aion” in 1990, before “Into the Labyrinth” brought the ethnic instrumentation to the front of the arrangements. A world tour in 1994 produced the live album and film “Toward the Within”, recorded in California. Gerrard issued her solo debut “The Mirror Pool” in 1995, then reunited with Perry for “Spiritchaser” in 1996, which topped Billboard’s Top World Music Albums chart. Sessions for a follow-up broke down in 1998 and the duo separated, with one track from those tapes, “The Lotus Eaters”, surfacing on the box set “Dead Can Dance (1981-1998)” and on “Wake” in 2003. Gerrard recorded “Duality” with Pieter Bourke; Perry released “Eye of the Hunter” in 1999. They reunited for a 2005 European and North American tour, documented across a series of limited live releases, then returned to the studio for Dead Can Dance’s ‘Anastasis’ on 13 August 2012. Perry sold the Quivvy Church studio in 2015. “Dionysus”, mastered at Abbey Road, followed on 2 November 2018, and the duo toured Europe in 2022. In 2025 Perry said he was working on a sequel called “Apollo”, with himself as the only musician. New material has since appeared on Bandcamp through the band’s own Holy Tongue Records: “Our Day Will Come” on 20 March 2026, “Death Cults” in April, and Dead Can Dance release ‘The Cicadas’ single via Bandcamp in July. Thirty-three years on, “Into the Labyrinth” remains the record that took the duo from the 4AD roster to the Billboard 200.

items.body: Krimea is an Italian duo formed in 2021 by Alice Taylor and Nick SoLow. Over the past few months, they have released three singles, all of which are included on this debut album. “Are You Human?” features 12 tracks largely inspired by relationships. From the very first notes, you can recognize the Electro-Pop influence that drives the duo. What also stands out immediately is the quality of the production and mixing. Krimea has clearly invested considerable time and expertise in creating a polished, high-quality record. The songs themselves are powerful Electro-Pop, yet they also possess a cold, atmospheric quality, incorporating vintage sounds and effects such as sweeps. Two songs are featuring guitar play. Certain sounds occasionally remind me of Kraftwerk, although this influence has clearly been transformed into a style and vibe that is uniquely their own. The vocal production is excellent, featuring a charismatic male voice alongside a warmer, ethereal female voice. She often provides backing vocals but occasionally steps forward for genuine duets. This is an interesting debut featuring several strong tracks. I look forward to hearing more from this duo, which, in my opinion, is clearly ready for a record deal. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Die-Monds”: “Die – monds” by Krimea About Krimea Krimea is an electro-pop duo from Venice, Italy, formed in 2021 by Alice Taylor and Nick SoLow. “Are You Human?”, released 10 April 2026, is the duo’s debut album, gathering twelve tracks written by Krimea and produced and mastered by William Benedetti. Guitar on “This Pleasure” and “Vivre le sombre” was played by Cosimo Mitrugno, with artwork photography by Matteo Bosi, per the band’s own Bandcamp credits. The album follows three singles issued ahead of release: “This Pleasure,” “Die-Monds” and “Over and Over,” all included on the final tracklist alongside nine additional songs. Bandcamp’s own album notes describe “Die-Monds” as built around the wordplay of “die” and “monds” (diamonds), with Alice Taylor crediting a vintage Poly800 II synthesizer for the track’s melodic range. No prior Side-Line coverage of Krimea has been found.

items.body: The piano has always occupied a peculiar position in contemporary music. It can function as a harmonic instrument, a melodic voice, a percussive object, or simply as a source of resonance and noise. In recent years, the felt piano has increasingly become associated with the latter possibilities: its softened attack and reduced brightness reveal a more intimate and fragile side of the instrument. Intimate Felt Piano, by Mondo Loops, takes this idea as its starting point, but rather than presenting the felt piano as a single predefined aesthetic, it treats it as a collection of textures that can be shaped by the player. The instrument is based on a double-felted Kawai KU3B upright piano, sampled across 88 keys with three velocity layers, pedal-up and pedal-down sampling, and up to four round robins. It is designed around a close, warm sound rather than the polished projection of a concert grand.  That choice immediately defines its character. An intimate piano The first impression suggested by Intimate Felt Piano is one of physical proximity. The instrument does not attempt to recreate the experience of hearing a piano from the back of a concert hall. Instead, it places the listener much closer to the mechanism. This is particularly evident in the way Mondo Loops treats the noises surrounding the notes. Felt noise, pedal release, hammer release, and room/player noise are all independently controllable. These elements could easily have been treated as unwanted artefacts of the recording process. Here, they are deliberately exposed as part of the instrument’s sonic vocabulary.  It is an important distinction. The noises of a piano are normally something that a sample library tries to reproduce convincingly while keeping them subordinate to the musical note. Intimate Felt Piano instead allows the user to decide how prominent those sounds should become. As a result, the instrument can move beyond the traditional idea of a piano library and towards something closer to a playable sound-design tool. Three ways of hearing the same instrument The library is organised around three sample sets: Felt, Tape and Mute. The Felt layer represents the most direct interpretation of the instrument: a double-felted upright with a soft and restrained response. Tape takes the concept somewhere else. The material is recorded to tape, slowed slightly and retuned, creating a denser and more nostalgic character. Rather than simply adding tape processing to an otherwise conventional piano, this approach makes the altered recording itself part of the instrument’s identity.  Mute is perhaps the most conceptually different of the three. The strings are physically muted, producing a tighter and more percussive response. Together, these three approaches make the instrument considerably more flexible than its name might initially suggest. They can be understood almost as three different perspectives on the same object: the piano as an acoustic instrument, the piano as a degraded recording, and the piano as a percussive mechanism. The sound between the notes The most interesting aspect of Intimate Felt Piano may not actually be the piano itself. It is what happens between the notes. The interface provides controls for Felt, Hammers, Pedal, Noise and Round Robin behaviour, alongside independent controls for the Room, Ribbon, stereo Pair and Pad elements. The microphone setup includes stereo condenser, ribbon and room perspectives.  This gives the user considerable control over the perceived distance and physicality of the instrument. A close microphone can make a sparse melody feel almost tactile. Increasing the room component can turn the same material into something more atmospheric. Mechanical noises can remain almost imperceptible or become an audible layer in their own right. For composers working with sparse material, this is particularly useful. When a piece relies on repetition, sustained tones, or limited harmonic movement, small changes in resonance and articulation can become structurally meaningful. The sound of a pedal being released or a hammer returning to position can provide information that would otherwise be absent from a perfectly clean MIDI performance. The imperfections are therefore not merely imperfections. They become parameters of the composition. From neoclassical to sound design Mondo Loops positions the instrument towards lo-fi, ambient, cinematic, and neoclassical music, and these are certainly natural environments for it. However, its possibilities extend beyond those genres. A felt piano is particularly effective when the distinction between instrument and texture becomes blurred. A simple repeated figure can be left almost completely dry and intimate, allowing the physical sound of the piano to remain exposed. Alternatively, the Tape or Mute material can become the starting point for further processing: granular synthesis, convolution, filtering, delay, or extensive reverb can transform the piano into something increasingly distant from its acoustic source. This makes Intimate Felt Piano potentially interesting within experimental and electroacoustic workflows as well. Rather than requiring the piano to remain recognisable as a piano, the instrument provides enough raw material to allow that identity to be gradually dismantled. Imperfection and repetition There is also something particularly appropriate about this approach in the context of contemporary minimalist and post-minimalist writing.Repetition inevitably draws attention to details. When the same harmonic or melodic material returns multiple times, the listener begins to notice differences in attack, resonance, noise and spatial perception. A perfectly identical repetition can sound mechanical; a repetition containing small variations can instead suggest the physical passage of time. The combination of multiple velocity layers and up to four round robins helps avoid a completely static repeated performance, while the dedicated noise controls allow the user to decide how much of the physical character of the instrument remains audible.  In this sense, Intimate Felt Piano is not only concerned with making a piano sound softer. It is concerned with making the process of playing the piano audible. A deliberately focused instrument There is a temptation with modern virtual instruments to judge them according to how many sounds they can cover. Intimate Felt Piano takes the opposite approach.It is deliberately specific. This is not a comprehensive piano collection intended to reproduce every possible performance style. Its identity depends on the particular combination of felt, mechanical noise, close recording, and restrained dynamics. That limitation is precisely what gives it character. Instead of attempting to replace a general-purpose piano library, it occupies a much more specific space: the piano as an intimate, imperfect, and malleable sonic object. At $35, Mondo Loops also positions it as an accessible addition for producers and composers who already own a conventional piano library but are looking for a more defined sonic personality. The instrument runs in the free Kontakt Player 8+, so no additional Kontakt purchase is required.  Final Thoughts Intimate Felt Piano is most convincing when considered not simply as another felt piano, but as an exploration of what happens when the secondary sounds of an acoustic instrument become part of the musical material. The soft attack is only the beginning. Felt, hammers, pedals, room ambience, microphone perspective and tape degradation all contribute to an instrument that can occupy several different positions between piano and texture. For contemporary composers, producers and sound designers, this is perhaps its most valuable quality. The piano does not have to remain a transparent vehicle for harmony or melody. It can become an object to be examined, repeated, degraded and reshaped. And sometimes, when the musical material is deliberately minimal, the sound surrounding the note becomes just as important as the note itself. mondo loops product page here’s a demo mede entirely Intimate Felt Piano: Davide Fasiello · Davide Fasiello – broken memoriesThe post Mondo Loops – Intimate Felt Piano: When the Piano Becomes Texture first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
