items.body: ■ 基本情報マン・レイは1890年8月27日、アメリカ・ペンシルベニア州フィラデルフィア生まれ、1976年11月18日にパリで死去した、写真家・画家・彫刻家・映画監督。出生名はエマニュエル・ラドニツキー（Emmanuel Radnitzky）。両親はロシア系（またはウクライナ系・ベラルーシ系ともされる）ユダヤ移民で、父はテーラー職人だった。一家は1912年、当時の反ユダヤ主義への反応として姓を「Ray」に改めている。生涯を通じて本名や出自について語ることを避け、「マン・レイ」以外の名を持ったことすらほとんど認めなかったという逸話が残る。ダダとシュルレアリスムという二つの前衛運動の双方で主要な役割を果たした唯一のアメリカ人とされる。■ 生い立ちとニューヨーク時代7歳頃までフィラデルフィアで過ごし、その後ニューヨーク・ブルックリンのウィリアムズバーグ地区で育つ。ボーイズ・ハイスクールでデッサンと機械製図を学び、画家を志すが、1909年にニューヨーク大学建築科への進学を辞退し、地図や広告のデザインで生計を立てながら独学で絵画制作を続けた。写真家アルフレッド・スティーグリッツの画廊「291」に通い、近代美術と写真についての薫陶を受ける。1913年の大規模展覧会「アーモリー・ショー」でマルセル・デュシャンやフランシス・ピカビアらのヨーロッパ前衛美術に触れ、大きな影響を受けた。1914年、ベルギー出身の詩人アドン・ラクロワと結婚（1937年離婚）。彼女を通じてマラルメ、ランボー、アポリネールらフランス詩に親しんだとされる。1915年、ニュージャージー州リッジフィールドの芸術家コロニーでマルセル・デュシャンと出会い、意気投合。二人はニューヨークにおけるダダ運動の拠点を作ろうと試み、ローズ・セラヴィ（女装したデュシャンの別人格）を表紙に据えた雑誌『ニューヨーク・ダダ』を刊行するなどしたが、ニューヨークでは運動として定着せず、1920年頃マン・レイはこの試みを断念したと語っている。この頃、絵筆を使わない絵画、既製品を用いたオブジェやアッサンブラージュの制作を進め、写真の技術も習得していった。■ パリ移住とシュルレアリスム1921年、デュシャンの勧めもあってパリへ移住。以後、第二次大戦中のハリウッド滞在期間を除き、生涯の大半をパリで過ごすことになる。パリでは生活の糧としてまず肖像写真の撮影を始め、雑誌の仕事で女性のポートレートを手がけるようになり、次第に前衛芸術サークルの中心人物となっていく。詩人ポール・エリュアールとその妻ガラ（後にダリの妻となる）、アンドレ・ブルトンら多くの芸術家をデュシャンから紹介され、交流を広げた。1925年、パリのギャルリー・ピエールで開催された最初のシュルレアリスム展に、マックス・エルンスト、パブロ・ピカソ、アンドレ・マッソン、ジョアン・ミロらとともに出品している。シュルレアリスムやダダの集団とは正式な会員というより「同伴者」的な緩やかな関係を保ち続けたとされる。彼はパリ滞在中、ジェームズ・ジョイス、ガートルード・スタイン、ジャン・コクトー、アーネスト・ヘミングウェイら文化人の肖像を数多く撮影し、ピカソ、ブラック、マティスら芸術家の作品記録撮影も手がけた。雑誌『VOGUE』や『Harper's BAZAAR』の仕事も引き受け、ファッション写真家としても高い評価を得たが、商業写真と自身の芸術活動は明確に分けていたと伝えられる。■ 写真技法：レイヨグラフとソラリゼーションマン・レイの名を最も広めた技法が「レイヨグラフ（Rayograph）」である。1921年から22年の冬、カメラを使わず印画紙の上に直接物を置いて感光させる、19世紀からある「フォトグラム」技法を独自に洗練させ、自らの名にちなんでこの名を与えた。ダダの詩人トリスタン・ツァラはこれを「物が夢を見る瞬間」を捉えたものと評したという。2025年9月から2026年2月まで、ニューヨークのメトロポリタン美術館（The Met）で、このレイヨグラフを中心に据えた大規模展「Man Ray: When Objects Dream（物が夢を見るとき）」が開催され、絵画、オブジェ、写真、素描など160点以上に加え、新たに修復されたダダ・シュルレアリスム映画も上映された。もう一つの代表技法「ソラリゼーション（露光反転現象）」は、1929年、当時弟子であり恋人でもあった写真家リー・ミラーとの共同作業中に、偶然の産物として発見されたという逸話が広く知られている。暗室でネズミに驚いたミラーが現像途中のフィルムに誤って光を当ててしまい、白黒が部分的に反転した効果が生まれたというエピソードだが、この経緯には諸説あり、真偽は定かではない。この技法を完成させたのはマン・レイとされ、以後彼の代名詞的な手法となったが、近年の研究では発見の功績の多くがミラーに帰されるべきだとする再評価が進んでいる。■ 女性たちとの関係：ミューズであり協働者キキ・ド・モンパルナス（本名アリス・プラン）パリ移住後まもなく出会い、1920年代の大半を共に過ごした恋人であり、モデル。代表作「アングルのヴァイオリン（Le Violon d'Ingres、1924年）」は、キキの裸の背中にヴァイオリンのf字孔を描き加えた作品で、19世紀の画家アングルへのオマージュであると同時に、「violon d'Ingres（アングルの趣味＝本業以外の道楽）」という慣用句にかけたタイトルにもなっている。この作品の実物プリントは2022年にクリスティーズのオークションで1240万ドルという、当時の写真作品としては史上最高額で落札された。キキは実験映画『理性への回帰』『人魚の星』にも出演している。リー・ミラー1929年に出会い、1932年頃まで恋人兼協働者として過ごしたアメリカ人モデル・写真家。当初は弟子・助手として迎えられたが、実際には1930年から32年にかけてのマン・レイの写真仕事の大半を彼女が担っていたとも証言されている。電力会社の依頼による作品集『Électricité』も二人の共同作業とされ、マン・レイはミラーへの献辞で彼女の助力への感謝を記している。しかし作品のクレジットは基本的にマン・レイ名義となっており、近年の美術史ではミラーの貢献の再評価が進められている。ミラーが去った後、マン・レイは彼女との破局のショックを反映した作品として、後述する「破壊されるべきオブジェ」にミラーの目の写真を取り付けている。アディ・フィデリン1934年末から1940年まで関係を持ったフランス領グアドループ出身のアートモデル。多くの写真作品に登場したが、2022年頃まで彼女の存在は伝記からほぼ抜け落ちていたとされ、近年になって再発見・再評価が進んでいる。マン・レイがナチス占領下のフランスを逃れる際、フィデリンは家族の世話のためフランスに残ることを選んだ。ジュリエット・ブラウナー（後のジュリエット・マン・レイ）1940年、ナチス占領を避けてロサンゼルスに渡った際、ナイトクラブで出会ったダンサー・モデル。マーサ・グラハムに師事した経験を持つ。1946年、友人であったマックス・エルンストとドロテア・タニングとの合同結婚式で正式に結婚した。以後、マン・レイの終生の伴侶となり、1951年のパリ帰還後もリュクサンブール公園近くのアトリエで共に暮らした。ジュリエットは1991年に死去し、夫と同じモンパルナス墓地の墓に埋葬されている。彼女は生前、マン・レイの作品の多くを美術館へ寄贈する慈善信託を設立した。■ 代表的な写真作品「アングルのヴァイオリン」（1924年）「ノワール・エ・ブランシュ（黒と白）」（1926年、雑誌VOGUEパリ版に初掲載。モデルはキキ、アフリカの仮面と顔を対比させた作品でアフリカ美術の翻案として美術史的にも重要視されている）「ガラスの涙（Larmes）」（1930〜32年頃、涙に見立てたガラス玉を顔にあしらった作品）リー・ミラーのソラリゼーション肖像（1929〜30年）メレット・オッペンハイム（毛皮のティーカップで知られるシュルレアリスト）が印刷機の脇でヌードになった1933年の連作■ オブジェ・彫刻作品「贈り物（Le Cadeau / The Gift）」（1921年）アイロンの底面に14本の裁縫用ピンを貼り付けたレディメイド彫刻。1921年12月、パリでの初個展オープニングで即興的に制作・展示された。オリジナルは失われているが、複製が各地の美術館に所蔵されている。「破壊されるべきオブジェ（Object to Be Destroyed）」／「破壊できないオブジェ（Indestructible Object）」（1923年制作、以後複数回作り直し）メトロノームの振り子に、目をくり抜いた写真を取り付けた作品。当初は無名の目（キキの目とされる）だったが、1932年頃、恋人だったリー・ミラーとの破局を受けて彼女の目の写真に付け替えられた。1957年、パリでの展示中に学生グループが実際にこの作品を破壊するという事件が起き、以後マン・レイは「破壊できないオブジェ」という新しいタイトルで複数のエディションを制作し続けた。ニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA）やスミソニアン・アメリカ美術館など、複数の主要美術館が版を所蔵している。■ 映画監督としての仕事マン・レイは1923年から29年にかけて、4本の実験映画を監督した。『理性への回帰（Le Retour à la raison）』（1923年、約3分）：セロファンに直接塩や胡椒、ピンなどを置いて感光させる手法や、キキの裸の胴体に光と影を投影する場面などで構成された、一夜漬けで制作された作品。『エマク・バキア（Emak Bakia）』（1926年、約19分）：バスク語で「私に構わないでくれ」を意味するタイトルの「シネポエム」。二重露光やソフトフォーカス、レイヨグラフなど静止写真の技法を動画に応用した。『人魚の星（L'Étoile de mer）』（1928年、約20〜27分）：シュルレアリスム詩人ロベール・デスノスの詩を基にした、キキ主演のほぼ唯一ストーリー性を持つ作品。『骰子城の秘密（Les Mystères du Château du Dé）』（1929年）：ノアイユ子爵の依頼で撮られた作品。2023年、これら4作品は初の4Kデジタル修復版としてまとめられ、ジム・ジャームッシュらのバンドSQÜRLによる新たな音楽をつけて「Return to Reason: Four Films by Man Ray」としてクライテリオン・コレクションからリリースされている。■ 第二次大戦、ハリウッド時代、晩年1940年、ユダヤ系であることへの迫害を恐れ、ダリ夫妻や映画監督ルネ・クレールらとともにリスボン経由でアメリカへ逃れ、ロサンゼルス（ハリウッド）に滞在。当初はタヒチへの移住も検討していたという。ハリウッドでは商業写真家として一定の成功を収めたが、本人は都市の刺激不足や、批評家たちが自分の多才さや商業写真での成功をうまく理解できないことに不満を抱いていたとされる。1944年秋、パサデナ・アート・インスティテュートで30年間の画業をたどる最初の回顧展を開催。1951年、パリへ帰還し、以後は絵画制作によりいっそう力を注いだ。1963年、自伝『セルフ・ポートレート（Self Portrait）』を出版。1976年11月18日、愛したパリの自宅アトリエで死去、享年86。モンパルナス墓地に葬られ、墓碑には彼が生前しばしば口にしていた言葉「Unconcerned, but not indifferent（無頓着であっても、無関心ではない）」が刻まれている。■ 評価と近年の展示動向マン・レイは自らを「何よりもまず画家」であると考えていたが、写真史・美術史上最も大きな足跡を残したのは写真の分野であり、20世紀写真の革新者として、リチャード・アヴェドンやロバート・メイプルソープなど後続世代の写真家にも影響を与えたとされる。彼のポップアート的な感性は、1960年代のポップアートの先駆けとも評価される。フランス国籍を取得したアメリカ生まれの美術家として、パリのポンピドゥー・センターやメトロポリタン美術館、MoMA、ゲティ美術館など世界の主要美術館に作品が収蔵されている。近年の主な展覧会としては、2025年9月から2026年2月にかけてニューヨークのメトロポリタン美術館で開催された「Man Ray: When Objects Dream」（レイヨグラフに焦点を当てた過去最大規模級の展示）のほか、同時期にミラノでも「Man Ray. Forms of Light」展が開催され、ファッションブランド（イヴ・サンローランやマルタン・マルジェラ、シアパレリなど）への影響も改めて注目された。日本でも新潟市美術館などで「マン・レイと女性たち」といった切り口の展覧会が開かれており、キキやリー・ミラーら「ミューズ」との関係性を軸にした再解釈が進んでいる。■ 言葉彼自身の言葉としてよく引用されるのが「私は写真に撮れないものを描き、描きたくないものを写真に撮る」という趣旨の発言で、想像や夢、無意識から来るものは絵画で、すでに存在するものは写真で表現するという、彼の創作観をよく表している。また「独創性とは欲望によって動機づけられた創造であり、複製とは必要によって動機づけられたものにすぎない」といった、独自性へのこだわりを示す発言も知られている。――【参考ソース（生きたリンク）】Britannica「Man items.body: Earlier this Spring, a post on Facebook announced the end of physical media for the venerable NotTwo label, then based on Warsaw, Poland. It came as a bit of shock and the comments that followed showed just how important the label was to many listeners. The message was also a bit cryptic, it was unclear if the label itself was shutting down entirely. This summer, we learned, happily, that there while there was indeed big change at label, as it now finds itself on the West Coast of the United States in the care of long-time label assistant Cezary Lerski, it is still very much alive. Please see the interview below to learn more about the transition. One Voice and Two Truths To kick off the re-launch of the label in its new digital-only guise, Lerski has released two excellent compilation albums curated from the label's deep back-catalog, One Voice focuses on solo performances and Two Truths on duos. Scan the names on the track listings and one is struck by the prominence of the artists, for example Simon Rose, Ken Vandermark, Barry Guy, Peter Brötzmann, Joëlle Léandre, Anthony Braxton ... and that's just a random pick. One Voice starts off with the intense blast of baritone saxophone from Simon Rose on the track 'Boxhanger'. It begins with such intensity that one wonders how it could develop further, yet it does with speed and precision. The track 'Dekooning' from saxophonist Ken Vandermark stands in contrast to the opener: restrained and melodic, its intensity is more conventionally jazz focused. For something completely different, bassist Marcin Oles' version of Ornette Coleman's 'Una Muy Bonita' presents at once an entirely recognizable tune that on one instrument captures the rhythm, melody and spirit of the tune. Two Truths is also a rich collection of duo performances that one may never have gotten to - after all, while having everything online and available all at once makes it possible to access, actually accessing it becomes a whole other problem. Starting with 'Productive Cough' from saxophonist Peter Broetzmann and percussion Joerg Fischer, there are obviously treasures within just waiting to be (re)discovered. This one begins with a no-holds-barred intro from the uncompromising saxophonist before Fischer comes crashing in. Eight minutes of heart-pumping free improvisation follows. On 'Conversation 1' from bassist Joelle Leandre and vocalist Lauren Netwon, the duo crisscrosses each others sonic paths, wrapping around each other until the distinction of bass and voice is futile. In another unconventional blending, woodwindist Anthony Braxton and bassist Chris Dahlgren offer 'Penumbra for woodwind(s) & bass(es) 1+1'. It is a low-register pummeling that uses electronics to grind the two instruments together. These two hand-curated compilations show some of the true bounty from NotTwo's back catalog. Each recording comes with detailed liner notes and links back to the source recordings, making entering this rabbit hole ever more enticing. One Voice (MW001-5) by Various Artists Two Truths (MW002-5) by Various Artists *** An Interview with Cezary Lerski: Paul Acquaro: NotTwo has been around for more than 30 years, founded by Marek Winiarski. You spent many years working there — what first drew you to the organization? Cezary Lerski: It goes back to the early 2000s, right around when iTunes first launched. I was producing a compilation showcasing the best of new Polish jazz at the start of the millennium, and I reached out to Marek by email to ask about featuring a track from his catalog. He said yes — Simple Acoustic Trio, who later became internationally known as the Marcin Wasilewski Trio through their run on ECM, got a spot on that 2-CD compilation. That first contact grew into something more personal. At the time, the whole model of music distribution was shifting online, and Marek — despite never really warming to the Internet himself, he genuinely avoided it, social media included — recognized that the label needed to embrace that shift if it wanted to reach beyond Poland. I think I was simply the right guy in the right place at the right time. I became, informally, "the Internet guy," and before long I was running all of Not Two's online sales, handling customers, distributors, and the whole digital side. I think it was a real relief for Marek — it let him step back from that and focus on what he cared about most, the editorial and artistic direction of the label. PA: As I understand it, you had an important operational role in the label, were you involved with the musical direction and release choices too? CL: Honestly, that's always been Marek's domain. The musical direction, the release choices — that's him. Where I did have a real role was as a kind of gatekeeper. As "the Internet guy," I was the first line for the enormous volume of submissions the label got from artists wanting to release on Not Two. So I was the one who had to tell a lot of well-meaning dentists that no, we weren't going to put out their girlfriend's reissue of the Ella Fitzgerald songbook (ha, ha). But when something genuinely caught my ear, I'd push it forward and send it to Marek with my recommendation. That's actually how I recall Szilárd Mezei first came to Marek's attention — and today we have ten of his albums in the catalog. PA: Did you ever think that you would be in charge of the label? CL: No. Honestly, that thought never crossed my mind. I saw my role only as handling the online side, sales, distribution — while Marek was always the label. His ear, his taste, his editorial vision built Not Two, you can't just inherit that by osmosis. Taking over wasn't a plan; it was more like being handed the keys to a car you'd only ever been the passenger in. PA: Moving to California is a major change for both yourself and the label, how did this come about? CL: That's actually always been a bit of a misconception — I didn't move to California for the label, I've lived here since the 1994 Northridge earthquake, with a few years back in New York City in between. California's been home for a long time; if anything, the label followed me, not the other way around. For Not Two, though, it really was a seismic shift — pun very much intended. We cut the ties to a lot of what had supported the label in Europe: the local fan base that had grown up around Marek and the label over decades, the brick-and-mortar distribution network, the festival circuit connections. All of that infrastructure that took almost thirty years to build in Poland and across Europe — we're now starting, from scratch, to build something equivalent here. It's early days. That's part of why the online side has become so critical; without that European backbone, digital distribution isn't just an add-on anymore, it's the lifeline while we figure out what comes next. PA: Do you think it will have an impact on the label? If so, in what way? CL: I think it already has, and I think it will keep having one. The most obvious shift is that we're now positioned to build a real foothold in the US — a market Not Two never had strong roots in before, despite the catalog being world-class. Free jazz and avant-garde have a dedicated, if scattered, audience here, and being physically present, able to go to shows, meet musicians, build relationships in person rather than only by email, changes the nature of those connections. There's also the practical side — being US-based makes it easier to work with American artists, US distributors, and frankly, US customers who'd rather not deal with international shipping and customs. And going digital-first out of necessity has turned out to be an advantage too; the label isn't tied to a warehouse or a single postal system anymore. PA: What is your vision for the NotTwo going forward? CL: The short version: stay true to what made the label matter in the first place — Marek's ear, that "free" part of free jazz, the refusal to follow trends or chase what's commercially safe — while building the infrastructure so that vision can actually reach people wherever they are, not just where it's easy to ship a CD. Concretely, that means a few things. Getting the digital side fully modern — proper distribution, a website and catalog system that does the music justice, so someone discovering the label today has as good an entry point as someone who walked into a record shop in Kraków twenty five years ago. On the physical side, I have to be honest — economics simply won't let us keep releasing everything on CD the way Marek did for all those years years. Digital will be the default going forward, with Bandcamp being our primary platform. But for special projects, the door is very much open — especially if we can move away from standard CD runs toward small-batch, on-demand, limited editions, whether that's CDs, vinyl, or even cassettes. It's a different model than the old one, but it lets us keep tangible formats alive for the releases that deserve them, without the economics sinking the label. It also means growing the US presence in a real way — not replacing the European roots, but adding to them, so the label has two homes instead of one. And it means keeping the catalog itself honest, so thirty years from now Not Two still means something specific when you see the name on a release. PA: Can you give us a tease of any upcoming recordings? CL: OK, I can tease a little. Fair warning though: this isn't necessarily going to be your grandmother's free jazz anymore. I'm getting a steady stream of submissions from artists working at the edges of avant-garde, pulling in influences from Krautrock, rave, psychedelia, trance — it's a strange and wonderful mix, and some of it is genuinely unlike anything currently in the catalog. A few personal notes, since you asked: I've got a real thing for cello right now, and I think you'll hear that creeping into upcoming releases. And unlike Marek, I actually enjoy guitar too — so don't be surprised if it gets a bit more room on Not Two going forward. What genuinely astonishes me is how many artists from all over the world are reaching out — practically every day — names most people, myself included, have never heard before. And the quality is often stunning. At the same time, I want to be clear: we're not abandoning the family. We have relationships with over 800 musicians already in the Not Two catalog, and it's always an honor when they come back to us with a new project. And I'll close with this: we've put together a compilation series pulling together the best of our roughly 350 releases, organized by format — “One Voice” is entirely solo performances, “Two Truths” is duets, and the series continues from there with larger and larger groupings. Each one draws across the whole history of the label, so you might hear something from the late 1990s sitting right next to something recorded 25 years later. The idea is simple: instead of asking someone to dive into hundreds of albums cold, we're saying, here's a curated front door — start here, find what speaks to you, and then go explore the deep end of the catalog on your own terms. Explore the NotTwo catalog at https://nottworecords.org/ Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Mala Fama‘s Río Cayápas and NXDLLI offer two complementary readings of the same journey. Both emerged from Esteban Farinango’s time in the Afro-Ecuadorian community of Telembí in Esmeraldas and were developed simultaneously, before OTONO label head Luis Clériga suggested presenting them as a double release. Río Cayápas stays close to communal music-making, while NXDLLI carries traces of these experiences into more abstract and introspective territory. Río Cayápas makes its intentions immediately clear. It opens with field recordings that place the listener in a specific environment before entering into what the liner notes describe as a dialogue with “local ethnic and autochthonous sounds.” Traditional rhythms from the province of Esmeraldas, recorded in the Telembí community, provide the foundation. Electronics work closely within this material, reinforcing percussion, marimba and voices until the boundaries between acoustic performance and electronic intervention become difficult to locate. NXDLLI turns towards resonance, atmosphere and slowly shifting textures, with rhythm largely receding from view. Recordings made in Esteban’s hometown of Ibarra filter quietly through the album, sometimes almost imperceptibly, particularly in “wakay”, “minervita” and “AMSA”. Environmental sounds become fragments of acoustic memory, retaining a connection to place even as their original context grows indistinct. Heard together, the two records continually illuminate one another. Río Cayápas foregrounds community, ritual and embodied rhythm; NXDLLI draws those experiences into introspective electroacoustic landscapes. Their shared sources make the differences between them all the more revealing. The accompanying remix collection demonstrates how much possibility remains within Mala Fama’s material. Each contributor finds something different in the originals. Entrañas draws out memory and dream; Omaar pushes the rhythms towards deconstructed bass; The Hissed finds unexpected harmonic warmth through ambient drum & bass; Viiaan turns birdsong into the principal melodic voice; Siete Catorce amplifies the ritual energy already embedded in the percussion; DNZA reveals surprising correspondences between Afro-Ecuadorian rhythms and footwork; and Quixosis dissolves the project into ambient resonance, bringing it close once again to landscape. Across both albums, traditional and electronic elements share the same musical space without settling into a clear hierarchy. Farinango allows percussion, marimba, voices, field recordings and electronics to interact until their respective roles become increasingly porous. Río Cayápas and NXDLLI trace the same journey through northern Ecuador from different perspectives, preserving the immediacy of encounters in Telembí alongside the altered forms those experiences assume through distance and memory. To trace the river back to its source, I caught up with Esteban over Zoom. NXDLLI and Río Cayápas explore the same path from two distinct perspectives. One is more closely linked to electroacoustic experimentation and ambient textures; the other foregrounds the music and rituals of Esmeraldas. At what point did you realize that this project needed to be divided into two releases? Was this an idea that was present from the beginning or did it emerge naturally during the creative process? My creative process isn’t linear. I never begin by thinking, I’m going to make an album. I’m always collecting sounds. Wherever I go, I record things that interest me because I’m constantly looking for material to experiment with. When I travelled to Esmeraldas and spent time in an Afro-Ecuadorian community, I recorded field recordings, instruments and all kinds of everyday sounds. From the beginning, I wanted to create something that captured the atmosphere of that place. A lot of projects combine electronic music with traditional music, but the two often remain separate—as if the electronics exist on one side and the traditional instruments on the other. I wanted to avoid that. My intention was to preserve the roots of the music while introducing just enough electronics to place it within a contemporary context. To me, that approach makes the music feel more alive. I love techno and electronic music, but sometimes purely electronic music can feel a little soulless. I wanted the electronics to support the traditional music rather than dominate it. At first, I was simply planning to make an EP. Around that time I received a grant from SAYCE—the Ecuadorian authors’ and composers’ society—which allowed me to develop the project properly. I initially wrote three tracks based on the material I had recorded in Esmeraldas. At the same time, though, I was recording completely different sounds closer to home. My grandmother would take me to waterfalls and perform prayers for my journey, surrounding me with flowers and blessings. I recorded her voice, the river, the birds—everything around us. Those recordings gradually led me towards another idea: creating long, ambient pieces built from atmosphere rather than rhythm. So I found myself working on two projects simultaneously. Then I met Luis Clériga from the Mexican label Otono. I told him about both projects: the rhythmically driven EP inspired by Esmeraldas and this second collection of ambient pieces. He immediately suggested combining them into a single release, with one side dedicated to the Afro-Ecuadorian, percussion-based material and the other exploring the more ambient, electroacoustic side. I thought it made perfect sense because the contrast between the two approaches actually revealed that they belonged to the same creative process. So, in the end, dividing the project into two complementary releases wasn’t my original idea—it was Luis’s. As soon as he suggested it, though, I realised it was exactly the right way to present the music. The Cayápas River and the Telembí community occupy a central place in both albums, but they never appear as mere backdrops or soundscapes. They become spaces of memory, ritual, and imagination. During your time there, was there any sound, encounter, or experience that decisively changed the course of the project? Everything was new to me. Even getting there felt like part of the experience. You can’t reach the community by road—you have to travel for almost three hours by boat before disappearing into the jungle. Once you’re there, there’s no phone signal. They have generators, but electricity isn’t available all the time, so you’re completely disconnected. At the same time, the place is incredibly abundant. Fruit trees are everywhere. You walk around, pick a banana, a mango or some cacao straight from the trees, go down to the river and start fishing. There’s a real sense of living alongside nature. But it’s also an extremely poor community. That’s the contradiction. Everything is beautiful, yet people have very limited access to basic services because they’re so remote. The government has largely forgotten them. What really struck me was meeting the local marimba maker. He’s a remarkable luthier whose instruments are highly sought after by musicians from outside the community. He harvests all the wood himself and builds every instrument by hand, yet he receives almost no recognition or support. Seeing that made me realise there was a political dimension to what I was experiencing. I felt incredibly fortunate to be there and to learn from them, and I also felt a responsibility to tell people how they live, what their music sounds like and what that community means—from my own perspective, of course. What impressed me most wasn’t just the landscape but the people themselves. In many ways they’re incredibly rich without necessarily thinking of themselves that way. They live surrounded by fruit, by the river, by music. People are constantly singing or playing drums, and music is woven into everyday life. They also have an extraordinary number of musical traditions connected to different moments of community life. During funerals, for example, women perform beautiful vocal chants that I would love to record one day. Unfortunately, when I visited there weren’t any ceremonies taking place, so I couldn’t document them. There are other celebrations where musicians travel along the river at night in boats, playing marimba and drums as they move through the water. They also have ceremonies where people dress in costumes made from leaves, preserving traditions that clearly trace back to their African heritage. What amazed me was that all of this exists just a few hours from where I live, yet most people in Ecuador know very little about it. That became one of my motivations for the project: to learn as much as I could and to show that this small country contains an extraordinary diversity of cultures that deserve to be heard. The visit itself happened thanks to a friend of mine, DJ Mamba System. He had already been there several times because he bought a marimba from the local luthier, so he knew the community well. You can’t simply book a hotel or arrange a visit online. You need to know someone. Families welcome you into their homes, often without expecting anything in return. My friend invited me to come with him, introduced me to everyone, and that’s how the whole experience began. They were incredibly generous people, and we became friends very quickly. So this might be a bit of a silly question, but do they have their own language? They speak Spanish, but some words and expressions in their songs come from Yoruba, reflecting their African heritage. It isn’t a language they use in everyday conversation, but traces of it survive in the music. What’s really interesting is that they share the region with an Indigenous community. I can’t remember the name right now (CHACHIS), but they’ve lived alongside each other for generations. As a result, some people also speak the Indigenous language, and the two cultures have influenced one another over a very long period. The history behind that is fascinating. A slave ship was wrecked off the Ecuadorian coast, and many of the enslaved Africans managed to escape. They fled into the jungle, where they eventually encountered the Indigenous communities already living there. From that point on, they shared knowledge, traditions and ways of life. You can actually hear that history in the music. Some of the melodic patterns in Afro-Ecuadorian traditions closely resemble those found in Indigenous music, so there’s this beautiful cultural exchange embedded in the sound itself. Did they find it strange that an electronic musician had come all that way to learn from them? Not really. To be honest, I don’t even think of myself as a purely electronic musician. I also play guitar and work with acoustic instruments, so our conversations naturally revolved around their music rather than mine. I did play them some of my work. They thought it was nice, but they weren’t especially interested in the electronic aspect of it—and that’s completely understandable. They simply said, “That’s cool. Thanks for coming.” What mattered much more to them was sharing their own musical traditions. They have an extraordinary number of rhythms and musical practices that very few people know about, and they’re genuinely happy when someone wants to listen and help bring that music beyond the community. In the end, that became my role: not to introduce them to electronic music, but to help make their music heard by more people. The remix album feels more like a continuation of the original project than a complement. Artists like Kelman Duran, Omaar, Siete Catorce, and DNZA take the tracks into unexpected territories. What criteria did you use to choose the collaborators? Were you specifically looking for them to reinterpret the material from perspectives very different from your own? The idea for the remix album came quite naturally because the original release was very short—it was only a cassette with a handful of tracks. Luis from Otono and I started talking about ways of expanding the project, and one of us suggested asking friends to reinterpret the music. It immediately felt like the right thing to do. I contacted the people I’m closest to musically and asked whether they’d be interested in remixing the EP. Rather than assigning specific tracks, I sent them the whole release and let each artist choose the piece they felt most connected to. I wanted everyone to work from genuine enthusiasm rather than obligation. Luis approached it from the other side. He reached out to artists through his own network, particularly musicians from Mexico, and he has a really good instinct for matching artists with material. In the end, it became a true collaboration—half through my connections, half through his. We also wanted to bring together people who have shaped what Latin American electronic music has become over the last decade. Fortunately, many of them are friends. Kelman Duran, for example, is someone I’m very close to. He came to Ecuador a couple of years ago and since then we’ve been constantly exchanging music and ideas. Siete Catorce is another artist I’ve admired for a long time. I think we’ve been in touch for more than ten years. I still remember hearing his music for the first time and thinking, “Wow, this is Latin American electronic music.” He was one of the artists who really opened that door for me. Luis also invited artists I deeply respect, like Omaar, as well as VIAAN, who is originally from Mexico and is now based in Berlin. Everyone involved already had a very distinctive musical identity, which was exactly what we wanted. None of the remixes tries to imitate the original tracks. Each one takes the material somewhere completely different while remaining connected to the spirit of the project. I think that’s why the remix album works so well—it doesn’t feel like an appendix to the original release. Every artist brings their own personality to the music, and the reinterpretations genuinely surprised me. You described these albums as a “message of Latin American unity.” At a time when much of experimental electronic music continues to look towards Europe or North America, your work draws on Indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian traditions without turning them into folklore. What does this idea of ​​Latin American unity mean to you, both from a cultural and a musical point of view? That’s an interesting question because the idea actually came out of a political situation. Ecuador and Mexico went through a serious diplomatic crisis after our current president ordered the raid on the Mexican embassy in Quito. As a result, diplomatic relations were suspended. There is currently no Mexican embassy in Ecuador and no Ecuadorian embassy in Mexico. Luis, who runs Otono, is Mexican, and I’m Ecuadorian. We were watching all of this unfold while working together on these records. For us, the project became a way of saying that, despite what governments are doing, we’re still family. We’re making music together, exchanging ideas and building something collectively. That felt much more important than political divisions. At the same time, Latin America is going through a difficult moment. Across much of the continent, right-wing governments are cutting support for culture while aligning themselves politically with North America and Israel. Cultural funding is often the first thing to disappear, even when basic public services are already struggling. We wanted these records to carry a different message: that beyond politics we share histories, cultures and values that connect us across borders. Our societies are also becoming increasingly polarised. Everything seems reduced to left versus right, with very little room for dialogue. Music can remind us that there’s something else worth protecting. Every country has its own cultural identity, but those identities also speak to one another. That’s what I mean by Latin American unity. For centuries we’ve looked towards Europe or North America for artistic reference points. We absorbed ideas coming from elsewhere and adapted them to our own realities. Over the last fifteen or twenty years, though, something has begun to change. More and more artists are asking themselves: “Who are we? What stories belong to this place?” We live differently, we think differently and we experience the world differently. It’s time we started telling those stories ourselves instead of letting other people tell them for us. For me, that’s what finding a Latin American voice is really about. Finally, could you tell me a little about Ecuador’s experimental and electronic music scene? Outside Ecuador, very little is known about it. Ecuador actually has a much longer electronic music history than many people realise. The great pioneer is Mesías Maiguashca, who moved to Germany and worked with Karlheinz Stockhausen and many of the leading figures of European electronic music in the 1960s and ’70s. He’s someone every Ecuadorian working in experimental music looks up to. The problem is that it’s still very difficult to make a living from this kind of music in Ecuador. Most people simply don’t understand it. If you’re making ten-minute electroacoustic pieces full of strange sounds, they think you’re either wasting your time or completely crazy. There are only a handful of people making this kind of music. Artists like Quixosis, Joaquín Cornejo and a few others are doing really interesting work, but we’re talking about a very small community. Recently I’ve also seen some exciting initiatives around field recording. There are artists organising hikes into the mountains where participants record environmental sounds, then come back together to process the recordings and practise deep listening. I haven’t taken part myself, but I think it’s a wonderful idea because it encourages people to engage with the sonic environment in a completely different way. Most of this activity happens in Quito. I live in Ibarra, a small town about two or three hours away, and the local experimental scene is almost non-existent. There are maybe ten people interested in electroacoustic music here. Everyone else is listening to reggaeton and going out partying—which is completely fine—but it means experimental music remains very marginal. I actually came to this music through metal. I grew up listening to the darkest and heaviest metal I could find, especially black metal. Ambient black metal eventually led me towards electroacoustic music, and suddenly I realised there was this whole other way of thinking about sound. Once I discovered it, I couldn’t stop experimenting. What keeps me optimistic is that Ecuador is full of sounds that haven’t yet been explored. The musical traditions, the landscapes, the different cultures—there’s an almost infinite amount of material to work with. Experimental music here is still a very small field, but I think that’s exactly what makes it exciting. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Otero Vargas has created an album that rewards attentive listening without demanding a prescribed interpretation. It is dark, textural, challenging, and surprisingly inviting. Beneath its fractured rhythms and unstable surfaces is an unusually thoughtful piece of electronic composition. Dissonance is a compelling listen from beginning to end and another strong statement from both Otero Vargas and Facade Electronics. Even the roughest textures contribute to the larger architecture Dissonance by Otero Vargas   There is something particularly compelling about electronic music that refuses to settle into a recognizable shape. Dissonance, the latest digital album from Mexicali, Mexico artist Otero Vargas, thrives on that uncertainty. Released by Facade Electronics, the album is a carefully constructed collection of tension, texture, rhythm, and atmosphere that continually seems to be moving toward resolution without ever quite offering it. The result is unsettling, immersive, and deeply rewarding. Otero Vargas is the alias of Julio Otero Vargas, a figure with roots in Mexicali’s early electronic music scene of the 1990s. During that period, he was part of the techno-industrial duo R2. After years away from the scene, he returned to making music in recent years, issuing self-released recordings as well as collaborations with independent labels. Dissonance marks his third release with Facade Electronics, a label that has consistently demonstrated an admirable willingness to seek out artists operating beyond the obvious boundaries of electronic music. That spirit is immediately apparent here. Dissonance does not feel designed around a particular genre template or production fashion. Instead, Otero Vargas approaches sound as raw material. Static, distortion, pulses, fractured rhythms, and shifting electronic textures are arranged with a strong sense of proportion and purpose. The music can feel chaotic on the surface, but underneath that apparent disorder is an impressive control of dynamics. One of the album’s greatest strengths is its use of tension. Sounds frequently appear to be suspended in an unstable state, with rhythms emerging and receding while layers of electronic noise gather around them. Rather than relying on conventional melodic development, Otero Vargas builds movement through changes in density, repetition, interruption, and texture. A pulse might establish itself only to become obscured by a growing mass of sound, while seemingly incidental electronic artifacts take on a structural role. Even the roughest textures contribute to the larger architecture :: There is a physical quality to these recordings that makes them particularly effective. The textures often sound weathered and corroded, as though the machinery producing them is itself being pushed toward its limits. Yet Dissonance never becomes an exercise in abrasion. There are moments of remarkable beauty buried within the harsher material, and these contrasts give the album much of its character. The quieter passages are not simply respites from the noise. They heighten the impact of what surrounds them. The press description of Otero Vargas‘ work as “visceral, instinctive, Lynchian” is fitting, particularly in the way Dissonance creates a sense of unease without depending on obvious cinematic gestures. The album suggests strange spaces and uncertain environments, but leaves enough room for the listener to construct their own interpretation. Its narrative is felt rather than explicitly defined. What makes Dissonance especially successful is the balance between instinct and construction. The sounds may originate from experimentation and improvisational impulses, but the finished album demonstrates a clear understanding of pacing and composition. Nothing feels randomly placed. Even the roughest textures contribute to the larger architecture. Facade Electronics continues to be a label worth following precisely because of releases like this. Rather than simply reinforcing established electronic music conventions, the Northern Mexico-based label continues to push into stranger, less predictable territory. Dissonance is an excellent example of that philosophy in practice. Otero Vargas has created an album that rewards attentive listening without demanding a prescribed interpretation. It is dark, textural, challenging, and surprisingly inviting. Beneath its fractured rhythms and unstable surfaces is an unusually thoughtful piece of electronic composition. Dissonance is a compelling listen from beginning to end and another strong statement from both Otero Vargas and Facade Electronics. Dissonance is available on Facade Electronics. [Bandcamp] Dissonance by Otero VargasThe post Otero Vargas :: Dissonance (Facade Electronics) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct ERR101: enabl.ed – IDM(R)ot I by enabl.ed   Clean Error label operator James Batista, a longtime IDM aficionado, continues to expand upon his enabl.ed moniker, a project that has spent years pursuing entangled electronics, glitch manifestations, and melodic fibers through another chapter, IDM(R)ot I. Detailed as ROTCORE, “developed to observe what happens to experimental music after its methods become part of a shared vocabulary,” Batista works at a high level of sonic fracture, clean errors, and digital misalignment, assembling a collection that “studies rhythm, synthesis, sequencing, sampling, digital processing, melodic behavior, structural irregularity, and intentional error.” Surrounded by a familiar cast of sonic crafters we tend to gravitate towards—ie. Cephlon, Romanowitch, Suumhow, Vaag, exm, rRine, Foel, Yaporigami, ENV(itre), Dragon, among others—enabl.ed finds its footing in disjointed rhythmic structures, where fifteen tracks lurch, stutter, flutter, and settle between lullaby tones and sharply articulated beats. Opener “initiate.rot.heirloom” immediately establishes this elegantly fractured language, allowing clipped rhythms and tiny digital disturbances to sit alongside softer melodic gestures. Batista’s sonic voice develops with remarkable consistency, even when the machinery catches on a few speed bumps, from the minuscule electro-entanglement of “rot.protocol\_113” to the roughened, shuffled beauty of “Reverb of a dead catalog.” Clean Error Records announces ERR101: enabl.ed — IDM(R)ot I, the next release in the label’s catalog and the beginning of a project examining the changing state of IDM through its history, production language and technological inheritance. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct throughout the album. Ambient threads seep through “time-stretched memories,” where audible fragments seem suspended just beyond recognition, while “There are ghosts in the sequencer” digs into micro-textural repetition, letting clicks, granular debris, and sequencing artifacts accumulate into their own strange atmosphere. Earlier IDM signifiers (ie. Arovane, Phonem, Plone) surface across “Machine Empathy,” and “Failed Futurism,” yet each track pushes those familiar forms through enough processing, interruption, and rhythmic skew to keep them unstable. Melodies appear, fracture, loop, and mutate rather than simply resolve. Closer “Every genre contains its own extinction” hints at an even more pronounced shift in enabl.ed’s signature. Orchestral strings emerge amid organic glitch scurries in the background, creating a grandiose bookend unlike Batista’s earlier sound sculptures. What begins as digital fragmentation gradually opens into something more melancholic and cinematic, occupying an intersection between soundtrack music and IDM while remaining distinctly interstellar, tactile, and absorbing. Perhaps this new ROTCORE strata marks Batista’s next transmission. Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. ┌───────────────────────┐ │ R O T C O R E │ │ ERROR > IMITATION │ │ MUTATION > MEMORY │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ░▒▓████▓▒░ //│\ /// ERROR \\ //// BLOOMING \\ GENRE_CORRUPTION : 87.2% RHYTHM DECOMPOSITION : 74.8% MELODIC STABILITY : 41.3% ARCHIVE DEPENDENCY : CRITICAL NOSTALGIA SATURATION : HIGH ERROR VIABILITY : ██████████ IDM(R)ot I is available on Clean Error. items.body: Visible Light did not try to produce an exact sonic replica of El Yunque, but rather focused on the aspects that impacted the musicians the most, just as a landscape painter can highlight aspects of a landscape that a straightforward photo cannot communicate as well. “An act of ecological connection” Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape by Visible Light   Located on the slopes of the Sierra de Luquillo Mountains in northeastern Puerto Rico, El Yunque National Forest is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest system. At almost 29,000 acres, El Yunque is one of our smallest national forests, yet it is also one of the most biologically diverse. For example, El Yunque hosts 250 different species of trees—about as many as are found throughout all our other national forests combined. Among other rare species, El Yunque provides one of the last remaining habitats for the critically endangered Puerto Rican Parrot. It also houses 13 of the 16 known species of the coqui frogs that Puerto Ricans have adopted as a symbol for themselves and their island. Yet a 2018 biological study found that global warming has reduced El Yunque’s arthropod (insect) biomass 10- to 60-fold, which in turn has led to corresponding declines in the lizards, frogs, birds and other creatures that feed upon these insects. Stunningly beautiful yet profoundly vulnerable, El Yunque serves as both a magnetic tourist destination and the home of the Indigenous Taino peoples’ chief god Yucahn (Yokahn). In February 2025, Minneapolis-based duo Visible Light visited El Yunque. Stunned by what they saw and heard, Amy McNally (cellist) and Matthew Hiram (sound artist) recorded many hours’ worth of nocturnal soundscapes in the forest and then shaped their own musical compositions in response. As Matthew Hiram wrote on his Substack, “the music was created in collaboration with El Yunque, as an act of ecological connection.” To me the resulting four-movement album feels like one extended meditation or deep listening event; it becomes difficult to tell where the natural sounds end and those of the human musicians begin. The album sounds almost like an acoustic version of the forest bathing contemplative nature walks that Japanese practitioners have introduced to the world. Calling the listener to pause and reflect :: And when Visible Light says they collaborated with El Yunque to make this music, they really mean it. In addition to the human instruments of cello, Moog synthesizers, rosewood alto flutes, sidereal gongs, brass singing bowls, and more, the voices of crickets, coqui frogs, and many other animals sing out on the album. And so do the voices of the plants themselves, captured by sensitive electrodes fitted to the plants’ leaves that pick up tiny electrical vibrations that are sent by MIDI to be processed and complemented, as Hiram has done on his solo albums like 2024’s Yucca Music.  Sierra de Luquillo begins with “La Oscuridad” (“The Darkness”), a more than 17-minute composition that is the longest on the album. Nocturnal keynotes of insects and coqui frogs take center stage, warmed by subtle cello and synth textures, calling the listener to pause and reflect on the peaceful beauty of wild places like El Yunque, to let it lighten and expand our souls. Later in the track the cello melodies sound almost in a call and response progression with the nocturnal animal voices, reminding me a bit of jazz musician and philosopher David Rothenberg’s famous duets with humpback whales on Whale Music. The next track, “Música de las Plants,” foregrounds plant voices. It begins again with the nocturnal sounds of coquis and insects, but now they sound closer, as if the listener’s ear is right up against the plants from which they are calling. Cello and synth melodies emerge and evolve subtly, almost like clouds passing in the sky above the forest. Then we start to hear the resonant hums converted from the bioelectrical signals sparking through the leaves of the plants. Developing slowly, the music moves at the more deliberate pace of the forest, not the heedless speed of the human world. Singing bowls add an ethereal, shimmering, almost spiritual layer to the processed plant vibrations. And even with all this emphasis on plant voices, those of animals remain foregrounded throughout, highlighting their importance and agency. Creating a tranquil, meditative, and spirit-expanding atmosphere :: “La Tormenta” (“The Storm”) focuses on a very common event for this tropical forest: rainfall, which it receives more than 6 meters (20 feet) of annually. On this track rumbling thunder and steady rain accompany the voices of coqui frogs, crickets, and other insects. I appreciate the percussive detail of individual raindrops colliding with leaves that emerges. Tasteful use of gongs extends the listener’s consciousness wider and deeper into the forest, helping focus our attention on darker aspects of the soundscape and how they resonate with our own inner spiritual depths—storms also roar within us at times, sometimes terrifyingly so, yet as with the outer rains in El Yunque, our own inner storms ultimately purify and renew us. I love how the coquis’ froggy voices sound almost joyous during the rainfall, reminding me of how the Prophet Muhammad described frogs as praising Allah with their croaks and cries. “Medianoche” (“Midnight”) closes the album. Here the insect and frog voices sound quieter, and the human synths and cello take center stage. The instruments do a lovely job expressing some of the uncanny, liminal quality of the midpoint of the night, which also holds the seeds of the dawn—a juxtaposition the listener can experience clearly on this track. There’s also a bit of a wistful feel to the cello, starting to bid farewell to this lovely wild and sacred place where even the local Indigenous Taino peoples did not traditionally dare to dwell for long. Rosewood flutes seem to express a kind of voice I wish we heard more of in the field recordings: the abundant bird life of the neotropics, complementing the cello in a lively back and forth that sounds like a vocal exchange between actual frogs and birds. The resulting warm sounds interspersed with heavy silences reminds me of how real animals listen to each other and to us just as much as we do them. Creating a tranquil, meditative, and spirit-expanding atmosphere, “Medianoche” makes for a lovely ending to this album. In the end I think Sierra de Luqillo does a great job of encouraging deep listening that can in turn cultivate a feeling of ecological connection, ideally leading the listener to practices of care and preservation. The compositions feel specific to this Puerto Rican place, with keynotes of frogs and insects and rain. Yet they also help the listener hear the importance of the natural places we inhabit wherever we are through newly attuned, more attentive ears. I also appreciated that Visible Light did not try to produce an exact sonic replica of El Yunque, but rather focused on the aspects that impacted the musicians the most, just as a landscape painter can highlight aspects of a landscape that a straightforward photo cannot communicate as well. Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Across its ten tracks, vocals function as much as part of the instrumentation as they do a traditional lead, with Hammerbell and John Winston Phillips giving each song its own shifting character. Vocal-led pop, soft electronic detail, and subtly off-kilter textures and movements The Friendliest Fight We Know by Oen Sujet   Electroacoustic experiments take a more upbeat, vocal-driven turn on Oen Sujet’s The Friendliest Fight We Know, a cascading electronic-pop album released on cassette in late July 2026. Across its ten tracks, vocals function as much as part of the instrumentation as they do a traditional lead, with Hammerbell and John Winston Phillips giving each song its own shifting character. Opener “Tap The Working Space” moves through lullaby-like memories and off-center electronic textures before “Second Service” carries that momentum forward. Hammerbell’s vocals glisten with a light, occasionally roughened edge, adding warmth without pulling focus from the electronics. “This Mind To This Thought To Go” taps into an early Broadcast and Lali Puna-like sense of bubbling electronics, keeping its fuzzy warmth intact as brittle bursts of synth-pop brightness push the song along. Near its close, “The Other Wears The Red And The Blue” brings a flowing, cinematic quality, while “Splinter Group” bookends the record with an art-pop/prog sensibility. Once a full-fledged band with several contributors, the duo now seems more focused on refining a delicately balanced electronic(a)-pop space with Hammerbell and Phillips at the helm. The Friendliest Fight We Know finds Oen Sujet working comfortably within those boundaries, shaping ten tracks that move between vocal-led pop, soft electronic detail, and subtly off-kilter textures and movements. The Friendliest Fight We Know is available on Bandcamp. The post Oen Sujet :: The Friendliest Fight We Know (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Untitled brings a form of fantasy music where society or environment is imagined in an advanced technological and scientific age exploring the universe, time, future tech, and humanity. The monstrous and crazy hypnotic repetitive sound is the art of the impossible, famously indistinguishable from magic, a way to test new ideas and take tomorrow. Everyone is here riding into the unknown Untitled by RGL   The sound of strange science fiction dreams and dramas creating whole universes of the mind, with mutant ambient guitars, synths and beats, Untitled showcases a wide-ranging sonic palette, such as abstract drones placed alongside rhythm-driven tracks, modern electronic music that explores deep philosophical and psychological themes, encouraging the constant listener to contemplate the kind of future that waits somewhere ahead. If we don’t innovate, something else will. Untitled brings a form of fantasy music where society or environment is imagined in an advanced technological and scientific age exploring the universe, time, future tech, and humanity. The monstrous and crazy hypnotic repetitive sound is the art of the impossible, famously indistinguishable from magic, a way to test new ideas and take tomorrow. Let’s get started. The opening track is “I” (2:45). I imagine a twisted clock with sparks flying, heavy echo, busy guitar clockwork and pulsing electronic splashes. We are heading out into the unknown, with no name. Traveling like this distorts time, the sunrise starts again, “II” (3:48). Once the beat starts the sense of motion pushes ahead. I see endless fields and the electronic drone, with visitors speeding over the rising haze of sunrise, endless flickering misty tall grass fields. We move on, into the swirling darkness. A hidden orchestra warms up slowly, one or two at a time, then more join in becoming a slow imperceptible development of the environment and atmosphere, “III” (4:44) is like a sun bath, just sit and enjoy. “IV” (6:28) has a mysterious opening, entering into a dark Funhouse, a nervous fast beat shadowed by drones and other strange things, with voices somewhere else, it is impossible to hear people talking, but there are clues. Perhaps now we are riding next to the engine, things start purring as if under the rhythm of the rails, feel the power, steady and sure. The forward motion starts again with “V” (5:23), a strange wet munching beat, bobbing in the void with others, we are not alone and they are hungry. There is also a flute, which fits in an odd twisting solo over the strange wet sloshy beat that chews along at a slow and dangerous pace. I see distant embers glowing at night :: “VI” (4:34) starts with the sound of wet rocks, or perhaps the surface of a large body of water when it is very quiet, I don’t know. Maybe I see distant embers glowing at night, an old campfire by a new lake, more new things come and go but the main thing is the pattern itself. There is a huge rainbow glow in the sky which dominates the imagination. Next, on “VII” (3:18), the call goes out. The darkness is thick. The drone of the searchlight as it reaches into the inky blackness covers the visiting Martian judges, who are mumbling quietly amongst themselves. For the final séance the beats pick up as we go along into the end of it all, “VIII” (5:04). Opening into a frosty sparkling shimmering sunrise, phantom drones sustain throughout. Soon a beat bangs into form, abruptly kicking and tapping, the rhythmic machine builds and builds. The force stays strong, the elements shift and fit into new forms, bringing a host of wanderers. Everyone is here riding into the unknown. RGL is a Tokyo-based producer known for his lo-fi house productions and analog-textured dance music, with releases on labels such as Diskotopia and Breaker Breaker. In 2025, he released his debut album, Touzan. He is a member of the producer collective COSMOPOLYPHONIC and co-hosts the radio program COOL RADIO with fellow collective member RLP. The result is a work that crystallizes RGL’s distinctive sensitivity to sound and texture. Untitled is available on ato.archives. items.body: Hana Stretton’s album tiarn is filled with the kind of hazy lo-fi arrangements that pull on the heart strings of sepia toned memories, fading Polaroid snapshots in sound of private moments and community life alike. It’s not crazy to learn that some old family camera footage is part of the inspiration behind these songs. A seduction to enter into, like sleep itself tiarn by Hana Stretton   Hana Stretton’s tiarn is an exercise in dream reverie and hypnagogic songcraft. It’s a twilight album set between the edge of waking and sleep, night and day. It’s soft cadences are like the allure of the ocean, a seduction to enter into, like sleep itself, it catches you unaware and before you know it, you are inside another world with its own rules, its own logic. The pieces for this, her sophomore effort, were crafted during a period of time while living quite alone near the Pacific Ocean on its Australian shores. It was her habit to go down to the water and swim in the blue of dusk. These azure dips overlapped with the winter whale migrations, and perhaps some of their songs seeped into her own mind and soul. Water keeps things in the flow and ideas for music swam into her during her ritualistic purifications in the icy salt water. On the walk back home the melodies would surface and she would record these as the evening progressed. It’s this naturalistic process that gives the album its striking yet elusive character. Ideas for songs, poems or stories can come in a flash and they can come strongly, but they slip away just as easily. Paying close attention to them by the constant humming, constant singing, constant courting of the songs that wish to emerge is no easy to task, but Stretton has managed to coax these pieces out of that creative borderland, where there is always the risk of them slipping away, and into this suite of recordings that have made them very much alive. Stretton was born in Canberra, Australia, between Sydney and Melbourne. Permaculture, that mighty gift of ecological philosophy given to world by David Holmgren and Bill Mollison was born in Tasmania. One of my favorite principles from permaculture is the idea to “use edges and value the marginal.” It’s on the margins where different kinds of ecological systems blend together. It’s in the margins where different kinds of musical genres blend together. Here those genres are ambient and folk music, creating an idiosyncratic lo-fi blend. Her inspiration, as noted before also came from the margins of ocean and land, and it’s this dreamy characteristic between waking and sleep I find so pervasive across these wonderful pieces.   Bits of environmental detritus permeate the arrangements which consist of strings, pipes, synth, what sometimes sounds like accordion, many things I cannot make out exactly because of the way they are mixed maximalizes a sense of immateriality. Whiffs of field recordings, captured conversation, rain or wind throughout. The art of field recording reverses itself :: Field recording is now a folk art. Not only in the sense that the great ballad preservers of the past such as John and Alan Lomax went out into the field with reel-to-reels to record folk songs, but now, when most anyone can record environmental sounds on the fly, field recordings of the ambience of everyday life. That’s when the art of field recording reverses itself once again from being something that had once been used to preserve vanishing ways of folk life to becoming a folk art in itself. Hana Stretton’s album tiarn is filled with the kind of hazy lo-fi arrangements that pull on the heart strings of sepia toned memories, fading Polaroid snapshots in sound of private moments and community life alike. It’s not crazy to learn that some old family camera footage is part of the inspiration behind these songs. Before she was born her family had lived in Japan in the ‘90s. A young family looks over valleys to the mountains beyond during the summer. Her parents had also bought a synthesizer they never used while in Tokyo. She started using that synth and it was a way to reconnect to the past. Some of the sounds from the camera footage also make up the field recordings that were used—the hushed conversations, the rain, the wind, insects buzzing. This is the place where family tapes and home movies form another kind of private documentary, a documentary now shared in all its vulnerability. “Yet I know these soundscapes and songs were composed even if it feels as if when I am listening, that I am just caught up inside of Stretton’s daydream. It’s not a bad daydream to be inside of, especially on a lazy afternoon” ~Justin Patrick Moore Isolationist piano tinkles meet lazily strummed, half strummed, barely strummed, guitars and other instruments that just seem to fall out of the speakers effortless. Yet I know these soundscapes and songs were composed even if it feels as if when I am listening, that I am just caught up inside of Stretton’s daydream. It’s not a bad daydream to be inside of, especially on a lazy afternoon. The group singing of the choir who collaborated with her on the song “As It Was Before This” is one of the points on the record where the tension between the individual and community is felt. The choir is reminiscent of heavenly realms and oceanic expanses. A sense of communion with powers outside the self is heard through these uplifting voices as they bridge material and non-physical realms. This feels like a very private album, very personal in its overall vision, aesthetic and design, yet I hear a longing for connection in these songs. Other players are here as well, other voices. Yet the mingle in with her own playing, her own compositions. The word tiarn means landholder. Stretton shows her ability on this record to be a songholder bridging the realms of ocean and land, dream and waking life, bringing back treasures from the deep to share with the world. tiarn was released independently in August, with vinyl editions through P.W. items.body: MEGAFAUNA creates a dark atmosphere using nature sounds and electro-acoustic manipulation to take the mind somewhere it didn’t expect to go. Listening to this at early morning hours, at normal volume, lying down, not fully awake, is a specific and disorienting experience. It’s quite amazing for what it is: a live improvisation built from birds that manages to sound like a horror score composed by the landscape itself. A strength in honest field recording work and a meticulous approach to effects Birdsong by MEGAFAUNA   MEGAFAUNA is a project based out of Hazelton, British Columbia, a small town in Northern BC’s Skeena Country, deep in a landscape of mountains, rivers, and boreal wilderness. Operating under the self-described tag “despairtronica,” the project has built a catalog of IDM-influenced and breakcore-adjacent electronic music characterized by hard drums, fast tempos, and dense sonic construction. A September release is on the horizon that will return to that territory. Birdsong is something else entirely, and that contrast is part of what makes it worth paying attention to. The field recording and bioacoustics tradition has a long and serious history. Bernie Krause—one of the foremost soundscape ecologists alive, has spent over fifty years recording natural soundscapes and coined the term “soundscape ecology,” documenting how the sonic layers of an environment (biophony, geophony, anthrophony) create a complete acoustic picture of a habitat’s health. The Cornell Lab of Ornithology‘s Macaulay Library holds over 175,000 audio recordings of wildlife going back to 1929, including the world’s oldest known wildlife sound recordings. Ornithological vocalization analysis—the study of bird calls for species identification, territorial behavior, and mating patterns, is a genuine scientific discipline. What MEGAFAUNA does here isn’t science. But it borrows from the same raw material and pushes it somewhere considerably darker. Birdsong was commissioned by circumstance, an invitation to perform at the Midsummer Music Festival in Smithers, British Columbia, with a specific request for something more ethereal than the prior year’s set. The response was a 42:42 improvised piece built entirely from bird call samples, performed live on July 4th, 2026, with rain and thunder added afterward to reflect what was literally happening before, during, and after the performance in real life. The track listing credits specific birds by role—percussion (Shoebill, Crested Caracara, Lyrebird), vox (Quail, Three Wattled Bellbird, Bearded Bellbird, Capuchin, Horned Screamer, Screaming Piha), ambience (Common Loon, Helmeted Hornbill, Pheasant Coucal, Tawny Frogmouth), melody (Raven, Australian Bustard, American Bittern, Common Starling, Magpie), and keyboard (Crow). Whether this is satire, creative taxonomy, or a genuine documentation of sources used, it’s a uniquely compelling framing device that makes the listener hear the piece differently, starting to identify what each bird might be contributing to the overall texture. What MEGAFAUNA shows with “Birdsong” is a strength in honest field recording work and a meticulous approach to effects, how carefully FX are applied to these recordings and how that compositional process produces something genuinely interesting. None of it is repetitive. These are natural sounds being manipulated very carefully with dark ambience throughout. None of the atmosphere on this release is pleasant, it presents itself as a dark record, which is also what makes it strangely unique. When you think of birds, darkness isn’t the first association, unless you’re thinking of vultures or birds of prey. But MEGAFAUNA pulls darkness out of unexpected sources. The Horned Screamer and Screaming Piha are doing exactly what their names suggest, and pitched down and ring modulated, they become something else entirely. The first two minutes present something resembling a rainforest, birds layering and overlapping in what sounds like natural habitat. Then around the 3:30 mark, things shift. The atmosphere darkens and stays dark, little bursts of FX being applied to various bird calls, distortions and pitching manipulations building until the 23-minute mark where something changes audibly. A pitch-bending melody arrives like an echoing alarm, a new segment of birds being introduced, the composition pivoting into its second movement. At the 27:40 mark, another sound surfaces that reads initially as an alarm but is clearly a bird call being manipulated—low pitched, ring modulated, buried under heavy reverb, looping in a way that creates something deeply unsettling and hard to source. It’s the kind of sound that makes you question what you’re hearing. The FX work is what really stands out, the ability to keep ears engaged with bird calls and sounds for 42 minutes without the piece becoming monotonous is a genuine compositional achievement. MEGAFAUNA creates a dark atmosphere using nature sounds and electro-acoustic manipulation to take the mind somewhere it didn’t expect to go. Listening to this at early morning hours, at normal volume, lying down, not fully awake, is a specific and disorienting experience. It’s quite amazing for what it is: a live improvisation built from birds that manages to sound like a horror score composed by the landscape itself. Birdsong is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the almost unanimously deemed disappointments that emerged from the German Krautrock meetsprogressive electronic scene surely has to be this little side project called LILIENTAL (LilyValleys) which was somewhat of an underground supergroup initiated by the great Dieter Moebiusduring some down time from Cluster. In writing it sounds like it should be the best album of thegenres with producer Conny Plank at the helm and a star studded team that included bassist HelmutHattler of Kraan, saxist and flausti Johannnes Pappert also of Kraan, synthesizer wizard Okko Bekkerwho was a solo artist as well as performing with A.R & Machiens and solo moog trippy AsmusTietchens. Together this team released one self-titled album in 1978 that featured ambientsynthesizer electronica, subtle rock elements and smooth jazz.This album features the ultimate mismatch of cover art and musical content inside with apresentation that suggests a glam rock or new wave type of album but rather delivering a trippy andheady journey through koschmische sequenced looping and and experimental avant-garde psychedelia.The album featured six tracks that added up to about 35 minutes and like most of this style of musicwas almost entirely instrumental however wordless vocal utterances such as the haunting chant-likeeffects on "Adel" do emerge albeit slightly imperceptibly. With four keyboardists at the helmincluding Conny Plank who performs as well as produces, the music is a tapestry of synthesizedgrooves and contrapuntal ambience which offers some interesting experimentation but nothingsubstantial different than what Moebius had been cranking out in other projects such as Cluster.This one is a mixed bag really. The first side is pretty good actually with "Stresemannstrasse"ushering in one of those classic hypno-grooves that streams on like a river of sound for a good fiveminutes. Like many Moebius projects the ambient surges are repetitive, soothing and meditative."Adel" follows and offers a few more shifts in dynamics that leads to an angelic "choir" effect atthe end. The track "Wattwurm" features a catchy melodic keyboard riff over a nonchalant space rockbeat that is the catchiest pop hook on board. SIde two begins with "Vielharmonie" which has an introsound that reminds of how Pink Floyd's "Dark Side Of The Moon" album begins however this track sortof sputters around and never develops into anything substantially interesting. The final two tracksdrift on into an ambient form of smooth jazz which totally destroys any momentum the album wasgenerating during the first half.As a side project this isn't overtly horrible but rather feels like a rather generic by-the-bookseffort made even more so given the high profile personal involved proving that often so-calledsupergroups suffer from watering down each other's strength rather than enhancing them. This soundsmore like a Moebius solo project than any larger group effort and the first side is actually verypleasant but the second side seems to just aimlessly wander and marred further by a Kenny G type ofsaxophone presence that probably prognosticated the advent of smooth jazz that was all the rage inoffice cubicles and elevators alike in the 1980s. Despite the ridiculously awful album cover, thefirst half of this album is pretty decent prog electronic while the second half i could more thanlive without. These guys wisely went their separate ways after this footnote in Kraut history.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — A band and a debut album i honestly have never gotten the hype about. SATIN WHALE like many was acollection of musicians that had previous histories and around 1971 found common grounds in joiningthe popular prog rock scene of the era. This is one of those bands that eschewed the headiest tripsof what was taking place in the world of Krautrock and rather opted for a more traditional proto-prog blues rock oriented style which while not totally unheard of during the late to the prog partyyear of 1974 certainly rendered the band a bit anachronistic when this debut DESERT PLACES wasreleased. The band consisted of Thomas Br�ck (bass), Horst Sch�ttgen (drums) and Gerald Dellmann(keyboards) in 1971 with guitarist Dieter Roesburg joining the ranks in 1972 making the band aquartet.The band emerged in the Cologne region of Germany which was the birthplace of a number ofinfluential bands such as Can, Triumvirat and Eiliff originated. Although somewhat original in howit wove together the guitar-oriented blues rock prog that spawned the earliest Krautrock sounds withan occasional jazzy touch, despite it all the band sounds more in line with what was happening inthe 1970-71 timeline than the waning year of 1974 in the prog paradigm. Essentially based on thebluesy rock style that had propelled the late 1960s into the 70s, DESERT PLACES seems to have anaffinity for revisiting those years without any attributes to really propel it into the next levelof development at the time. This is essentially one of those albums that's pleasant to listen to butkeeps you wishing that it would all go somewhere more interesting . The album was released on Brain Records which also was instrumental in acts such as Klaus Schulze,Spirogyra, Caravan, Atomic Rooster, Khan, NEU!, Grobschnitt, Guru Guru and even early Scorpions.Well, you get the picture. SATIN WHALE just wasn't up to par with these other innovative forces inthe German Kraut scene although nothing on the album is offensively substandard in any way. Thevocalist is competent, the music is listenable and it offers nothing to grossly offend but yet itseems a bit underwhelming in comparison to the multitude of brilliant acts that were emerging duringthe time and place even within the locality of the German market itself. German criticism has alsoexpressed similar views with this band really failing to offer anything innovative or declarative inits essence. Overall it's an album that offers that perfect glimpse of 1969-70 only several years later. If it'sa style you find most appealing it's all fine and dandy but even taken at those standards it reallydoesn't excel at anything. The keyboards sound woefully dated, the musicianship while competentdoesn't ever deliver anything beyond competent and the album is rather dull if you're expecting oneof those furthest out there tripping types of music that Krautrock was extremely adept at crafting.Of course this is all subjective and many have deemed this album extremely exhilarating but forthose who want something a bit more idiosyncratic in their Krautrock experience then it does seem tobe a bit of a let down especially upon multiple listening experiences. For a more competent similarstyled band that sounded dated but still excelled beyond the basics in many ways, check out TwentySixty Six and then.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A multitude of images flood my mind upon hearing the opening notes of "St. Radigunds", evoking the arid, stripped-down atmosphere of a Western, or the German band Hoelderlin in their initial incarnation as H�lderlins Traum (1972). Yet, although Spirogyra began as a duo, just like the Incredible String Band, it started as a trio, it was as a quartet (augmented by guest friends) that they truly took shape after Martin Cockerham, their founding guitarist, returned from the University of Kent in Canterbury.The guest lineup included drummer Dave Mattacks, so it is hardly surprising to detect traces of Fairport Convention's mysticism in this debut. The music strikes a balance between a powerful, distinctive acoustic sound and a prominent electric bass presence, courtesy of Steve Borrill."The Future Won't Be Long," the opening track, shines thanks to Martin Cockerham's vocals, reminiscent of Bob Dylan, and Julian Cusack's violin. There is a touch of psychedelia in "Island"; the acoustic guitar and violin weave an atmosphere that envelops Cockerham's voice, showcasing a technical virtuosity that serves the music without overshadowing it, yet remains present to provide dramatic tension."Magical Mary" is fascinating because the meter shifts to accommodate the vocals before speeding up, lending the song an uncanny spirit; the interplay between the violin and the electric bass provides a brilliant highlight where classical music meets Celtic influences. The tempo accelerates to a peak that brushes against psychedelia, until a second section begins, bursting with originality, showcasing the voice of Barbara Gaskin, the Grace Slick the band had kept under wraps.That subversion of time continues in "Captain's Log," while Dylan's tone also colors that rocky seascape. One foot in the '60s and Beatles-esque baroque trumpet arrangements in "At Home In The World." Returning to the stripped-down landscape of Cogwheels, Crutches and Cyanide, which reminded me somewhat of The Waterboys, given that Spyro Gyra would also leave behind heirs to their distinctive style, the combined vocals of Barbara Gaskin and Martin Cockerham blended beautifully, lending even greater power to the composition."Time Will Tell" also surprises with unexpected shifts, and the bass plays off the piano, played here by Julian Cusack. From complexity and intricacy to the simplicity and beauty of "Love Is A Funny Thing", where Barbara channels Sandy Denny, the sense of balance is welcome.A rhythmic, steady groove infuses "The Duke of Beaufoot", a track that is also highly progressive, evoking a world of ivy-clad walls and statues bathed in moonlight; it speaks of taking a moment to pause time itself, a square featuring a sundial or a cistern serving as a reminder of the past, while that guitar, bass, and steady violin line bring it all back to mind.
